You manage an Azure App Service application called PortalApp.

The development team plans to publish updates to PortalApp using Web Deploy. They must be able to

authenticate using their Microsoft Entra ID accounts when deploying the application.

The solution must follow the principle of least privilege and avoid granting excessive permissions.

Which action should you take?

options.A: Grant the developers the Owner role on the web app.
options.D: Assign the Website Contributor role to the developers.

explanation: Assign the Website Contributor role to the developers is the correct answer here. The Website Contributor role provides the necessary permissions to manage the web app, including deploying content, without giving the developers excessive privileges such as those granted by the Owner role. This ensures the solution follows the principle of least privilege. Grant the developers the Owner role on the web app is incorrect because the Owner role gives full control over the resource, including the ability to delete or modify access permissions, which violates the principle of least privilege. Set up application-level FTPS credentials is incorrect because using app-level credentials does not involve using Microsoft Entra credentials and does not follow the principle of least privilege. Configure user-specific FTPS credentials is incorrect because this does not involve using Microsoft Entra credentials and provides too much access for just deploying content.

following table.

Name In storage account Contains blob

------- ------------------- ---------------

cont1 storage1 blob1

cont2 storage1 blob2

cont1 storage2 blob3

Each container resides in a specific storage account and contains one blob.

The subscription includes two users named User1 and User2. Both users are assigned the Reader role

at the Sub1 subscription scope.

You have defined a condition named Condition1 with the following logic:

• The condition evaluates to true when the requested action is not a blob read operation

OR

• The container name equals cont1

You have also defined a second condition named Condition2 with the following logic:

• The condition evaluates to true when the requested action is not a blob write operation

OR

• The blob path matches a pattern that contains the value 2

You then assign roles to the users:

• User1 is assigned the Storage Blob Data Reader role at the Sub1 scope with Condition1 applied.

• User2 is assigned the Storage Blob Data Owner role at the storage1 account scope with Condition2

applied.

True or False:

"User1 can read blob2."
explanation: False is correct because User1 is assigned the Storage Blob Data Reader role at the Sub1 scope with Condition1, which restricts access to the blobs unless certain conditions are met. Condition1 specifies that User1 can only read blobs within containers named cont1. Since blob2 is in container cont2, User1 cannot read it due to the condition restricting access to containers named cont1.

You have two Azure virtual machines as shown in the following table. Each virtual machine runs a

different operating system, has both private and public IP addresses assigned, and is connected to the

same virtual network. One virtual machine has a DNS suffix configured in the operating system, while

the other does not.

You then create the following Azure DNS resources:

• A public DNS zone named contoso.com

• A private DNS zone named fabrikam.com

You perform the following actions:

• For fabrikam.com, you create a virtual network link to vnet1 and enable automatic registration.

• For contoso.com, you assign the Owner role to both vm1 and vm2.

True of False:

"The DNS A record for vm1 is created in contoso.com and resolves to the IP address 131.107.50.20."
explanation: False is correct because the contoso.com zone is a public DNS zone, not a private DNS zone. Auto registration for DNS records is supported only for private DNS zones when linked to virtual networks. Since contoso.com is a public DNS zone and auto registration is not enabled for public zones, a DNS A record for vm1 will not be automatically added with its public IP address of 131.107.50.20. Additionally, the assignment of the Owner role to vm1 and vm2 does not influence DNS auto registration, as that pertains to role-based access control (RBAC) and not DNS management.

You manage an Azure Storage account named dataarchive01, which contains a blob container

called images. This container holds a a large collection of image files.

You plan to deploy an Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template to configure a blob inventory rule

named inventoryRule1.

The configuration must ensure that a daily inventory report is generated in CSV format and stored in

the images container. The report must include only those blobs whose names start with the

prefix "finance".

You need to complete the configuration of rule1, shown below.

Which value should you choose for Code Segment A?
explanation: blockBlob is the correct answer. Block blobs are designed to store large amounts of unstructured data, such as images or backups, which is the use case described here with thousands of image files. Additionally, block blobs are more suitable for use cases where data needs to be frequently accessed, stored, or replaced (such as in a daily CSV file). This fits the requirements for the blob inventory rule where you need to filter blobs whose names start with "finance." appendBlob is incorrect because it is generally used for log data where the need is to continuously append new data. It is not optimized for image storage or daily CSV storage. pageBlob is incorrect because page blobs are typically used for storing virtual hard disks (VHDs) for Azure virtual machines, not for storing images or daily CSV files.

question:
You manage an Azure Storage account named dataarchive01, which contains a blob container

called images. This container holds a a large collection of image files.

You plan to deploy an Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template to configure a blob inventory rule

named inventoryRule1.

The configuration must ensure that a daily inventory report is generated in CSV format and stored in

the images container. The report must include only those blobs whose names start with the

prefix "finance".

You need to complete the configuration of rule1, shown below.

Which value should you choose for Code Segment B?
explanation: images/finance is the correct answer. According to the documentation, the prefix match string in a blob policy must always start with the container name followed by the desired blob name prefix. In this case, "images" is the container, and "finance" is the required blob prefix, making images/finance the appropriate match string for blobs starting with the word "finance." images/* is incorrect because it would match all blobs within the container and not only those starting with "finance." finance is incorrect because it does not include the container name as required by the blob policy format.

question:
You manage an Azure Storage account called mediafiles01 that contains a collection of image blobs.

You plan to provision an additional storage account and configure object replication to copy the existing

images from mediafiles01 to the new account.

After creating and configuring the destination storage account, you need to determine the appropriate

object type that must be created within it to support object replication.

Which object type should you create in the destination storage account?
explanation: Container is the correct answer here. Azure Object Replication is a feature of Azure Blob Storage, and it works at the container level. To replicate blobs from one storage account to another, you must configure object replication policies between source and destination containers. This means that in the new storage account, you must create a container, as it's the fundamental object that holds blobs (such as images in this case). Without a container, the replication policy cannot be configured or function. File share is incorrect because object replication does not support Azure Files. File shares are used in Azure Files, which is a completely separate service from Blob Storage, and is not part of object replication capabilities. Table is incorrect because Azure Table storage is used for NoSQL structured data, and again, object replication only applies to block blobs in containers, not table data. Queue is incorrect because Azure Queue Storage is designed for messaging between application components. It is not related to blob storage or object replication and cannot be used for replicating blob data.

You plan to provision an additional storage account and configure object replication to copy the existing

images from mediafiles01 to the new account.

After creating and configuring the destination storage account, you need to determine the appropriate

object type that must be created within it to support object replication.

Which account type should you create in the destination storage account?
explanation: StorageV2 or BlobStorage only is correct because object replication is supported by both general- purpose v2 storage accounts (StorageV2) and premium block blob storage accounts (BlobStorage). These account types meet the requirements for object replication, allowing replication of blobs between the source and destination accounts. StorageV2 only is incorrect because while StorageV2 supports object replication, premium block blob storage accounts (BlobStorage) also support object replication, and they should not be excluded from the correct answer. StorageV2 or FileStorage only and StorageV2, BlobStorage, or FileStorage are incorrect because FileStorage accounts do not support blob storage, which is necessary for object replication.

Other issues like missing Azure Container Instance permissions, registry access policies, or image tags could prevent deployment. A more appropriate solution would be ensuring that the container instance has the proper permissions to pull images from the registry. This can be done by checking if the container instance has the necessary identities (system-assigned or user-assigned) and permissions to access the container registry.

Proposed solution: Move the VM to a different resource group from the Overview balde.

Does this solution meet the requirement?
explanation: No is the correct answer here. Moving a virtual machine to a different resource group does not change the physical host on which the VM is running. The operation is a metadata-level move within Azure Resource Manager, and the underlying compute resources (including the physical host) remain unchanged. Since the goal is to move ProdVM01 to a different host immediately (e.g., to avoid upcoming planned maintenance), simply moving the VM to a different resource group does not meet the requirement. To move a VM to a different host, you must perform an operation that redeploys the VM, such as using the Redeploy option from the Azure portal or running the az vm redeploy command. This action will provision the VM on a new physical host.

Since the goal is to move ProdVM01 to a different host immediately (to avoid disruption due to planned maintenance), this solution does not meet the requirement. question:
An Azure subscription includes a container group named Group1. The container group hosts two Azure

container instances, as detailed in the following table.

Each container has defined CPU resource requests and limits.

You must ensure that each container cannot consume more CPU resources than it requests, and that

cont2 does not negatively affect cont1.

What action should you take?

options.A: Increase the CPU resource limit for cont1 to three CPUs.
options.B: Increase the CPU resource limit of cont2 to six CPUs.
options.C: Remove the CPU resource limits configured on both containers.
options.D: Reduce the CPU resource limit of cont2 to two CPUs.

explanation: Remove the CPU resource limits configured on both containers is the correct answer. Azure Container Instances allocates CPU resources to a container group based on the sum of the containers' resource requests. If no resource limit is specified for a container, its maximum CPU usage is equal to its resource request. Therefore, after removing the limits, cont1 cannot use more than its requested 2 CPUs, and cont2 cannot use more than its requested 3 CPUs. This ensures that neither container can consume CPU resources beyond its request and that cont2 cannot use additional shared CPU resources at the expense of cont1. Reduce the CPU resource limit of cont2 to two CPUs is incorrect because a container's resource limit must be equal to or greater than its resource request. Since cont2 requests 3 CPUs, its limit cannot be reduced to 2 CPUs. Increase the CPU resource limit of cont2 to six CPUs is incorrect because a container's resource limit cannot exceed the total CPU resources allocated to the container group. The group is allocated 5 CPUs based on the combined requests of cont1 and cont2. Increasing cont2's limit would also work against the requirement to prevent it from consuming more CPU than it requests. Increase the CPU resource limit for cont1 to three CPUs is incorrect because this would allow cont1 to consume more CPU than its requested 2 CPUs. It would not ensure that each container is restricted to its resource request and could increase resource contention within the group.

• A Recovery Services vault named VaultB

• Disk01 - Disk

• WebApp01 - Azure App Service web application

• SQLDB01 - Azure SQL Database

You plan to configure backup protection for these resources.

Which of the listed resources can be backed up using VaultA (the Azure Backup vault)?
explanation: Disk01 is correct because Azure managed disks are backed up using Azure Disk Backup, which requires an Azure Backup vault. This allows disks to be backed up independently without backing up the entire virtual machine. VM01 could also be backed up, but the backup would include the entire virtual machine, not just the disk. The question specifically focuses on backing up a resource like Disk1. WebApp01 (Azure App Service web app) and SQLDB01 (Azure SQL Database) have different built-in backup features and are not backed up directly using Azure Backup.

explanation: A route table that has custom routes is the correct answer here. To ensure that the traffic from VNet1 to VNet2 is inspected by NetVA1, you need to use a custom route in the route table. You can create a route that forces traffic from VNet1 to pass through the Network Virtual Appliance (NetVA1) for inspection before it reaches VNet2. This is achieved by setting the next hop in the custom route to the IP address of NetVA1. Configure a local network gateway is incorrect because it is used for configuring connections between an Azure virtual network and an on-premises network, not for routing traffic between peered virtual networks. Enable a service endpoint is incorrect because service endpoints provide secure access to Azure services but are not used for routing traffic through a Network Virtual Appliance. Configure IP address reservations is incorrect because IP reservations are used to reserve public IP addresses, and they do not help with routing or traffic inspection between virtual networks.

Once the managed identity is created, it can be granted the necessary permissions to access the Key Vault and retrieve secrets. You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that contains two users named User1 and User2.

You must assign Azure role-based access control (RBAC) roles to both users so they can perform the

following actions within Sub1:

• User1 must view the data in any storage account.

• User2 must assign users the Contributor role for storage accounts.

The assignment must follow the principle of least privilege.

Which RBAC role should you assign to User 1?
explanation: Reader and Data Access is the correct role to assign to User1. This role provides read-only access to management operations (like the standard Reader role), but also adds the ability to read the data inside Azure Storage containers and blobs, queues, tables, and files. This aligns perfectly with the requirement that User1 must be able to view the data in any storage account, without allowing write or management capabilities. It also adheres to the principle of least privilege, as it grants exactly what is required and nothing more. Owner is incorrect because it grants full access to manage all resources, including access management permissions. This is far more than what User1 needs just to view storage data, and violates the principle of least privilege. Contributor is incorrect because while it allows full management of resources, it does not grant access to the underlying data in storage accounts (like reading blob contents). So it's not sufficient for User1's data access requirement, and it overgrants permissions on the management plane. Storage Account Contributor is incorrect because it provides management access to storage accounts (e.g., configuring settings, managing firewalls), but it does not grant data plane access (like reading blobs or files). Therefore, this role does not meet User1's requirement to view the data inside storage accounts. User Access Administrator is incorrect because it allows managing role assignments, not accessing data. This role is relevant for User2's requirement, but not for User1. It provides no data access or management access to storage resources, so it is not applicable here.

explanation: User Access Administrator is the correct role to assign to User2. This role allows a user to manage role assignments in Azure RBAC, including assigning others roles such as Contributor. It does not grant permissions to manage resources directly, making it ideal when the sole requirement is to delegate access control, as is the case here. Since User2 needs to assign users the Contributor role for storage accounts, User Access Administrator provides precisely the needed capability while following the principle of least privilege. Owner is incorrect because although it allows full access to resources and access management, it overgrants permissions by allowing the user to create, delete, and manage any resource, which goes beyond just assigning RBAC roles. This violates the principle of least privilege. Contributor is incorrect because this role allows managing Azure resources, but does not include permission to assign roles to other users. Therefore, it cannot fulfill the requirement to assign the Contributor role to others. Reader and Data Access is incorrect because it only grants read access to Azure resources and data (e.g., in storage accounts), but does not provide any permissions related to role assignments or resource management. Storage Account Contributor is incorrect because it grants permissions to manage storage accounts, including configuration, but it does not allow role assignments. It does not fulfill the need for User2 to assign RBAC roles to others.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that includes a storage account hosting website content.

You need to ensure that users accessing the website are routed through the Microsoft point-of-

presence (POP) that is geographically closest to them.

What configuration should you implement to meet this requirement?
explanation: Routing preference is the correct answer. In Azure Storage, the routing preference setting allows you to specify how user traffic reaches your storage account; either through the Microsoft global network or over the public internet. To ensure that inbound user traffic uses the Microsoft point-of-presence (POP) closest to the user's location, you should configure the routing preference to use Microsoft network routing (also called "Microsoft edge network"). This ensures that user traffic enters the Microsoft network at the POP closest to the user's location and is routed through Microsoft's backbone to the storage account, optimizing performance and reducing latency. Load balancing is incorrect because while Azure Load Balancer distributes traffic across virtual machines and services, it does not apply to Azure Storage accounts or influence the routing behavior of traffic to them. Azure Firewall rules is incorrect because Azure Firewall is used for controlling and monitoring traffic to/from Azure resources, based on configured rules. It is not responsible for routing user traffic through the Microsoft POPs or determining how traffic enters the Microsoft network. Private endpoints is incorrect because they are used to provide private connectivity to Azure services over a virtual network. While they enhance security by avoiding public internet exposure, they do not control whether traffic is routed through the Microsoft edge network or influence the POP usage.

explanation: containers and queues only is the correct answer. Azure supports Azure role assignment conditions for Blob Storage containers and Queue Storage. This means you can apply conditional access controls —such as limiting access by IP address, resource tags, or actions—when assigning RBAC roles to these services. This feature enhances fine-grained access control, enabling you to enforce least privilege principles more effectively. file shares only is incorrect because Azure Files currently does not support role assignment conditions. You can assign roles, but not with conditional logic. tables only is incorrect because Azure Table storage does not support RBAC role assignment conditions. Access is typically controlled through account-level keys or Shared Access Signatures (SAS), not conditional RBAC. queues only is incorrect because while queue services support conditional role assignments, selecting this option alone ignores the fact that containers (Blob storage) are also supported. containers only is incorrect for the same reason—it's incomplete. Both containers and queues support conditional role assignments, so the correct answer must include both. file shares and tables only is incorrect because neither of those services supports conditional access using RBAC role assignments.

question:

options.B: The App Service plan for CustomerWeb01 remains in West Europe. Pol1 applies to CustomerWeb01.

options.E: The App Service plan for CustomerWeb01 moves to North Europe. Pol1 applies to

explanation: The App Service plan for CustomerWeb01 remains in West Europe. Pol2 applies to CustomerWeb01 is the correct answer here. When you move a resource like a web app to a different resource group, the region of the resource does not change—it stays in the same physical location unless explicitly redeployed. Therefore, CustomerWeb01 and its App Service plan will remain in West Europe. However, after the move, the policy assigned to the destination resource group (ResGrp2) will now govern CustomerWeb01. Since CustomerWeb01 is now in ResGrp2, Pol2 applies to it. The App Service plan for CustomerWeb01 moves to North Europe. Pol2 applies to CustomerWeb01 is incorrect because the App Service plan does not change regions automatically during a resource group move. The App Service plan for CustomerWeb01 remains in West Europe. Pol1 applies to CustomerWeb01 is incorrect because although the location remains unchanged, the applied policy comes from the new resource group (ResGrp2), not the original one. The App Service plan for CustomerWeb01 moves to North Europe. Pol1 applies to CustomerWeb01 is incorrect for both reasons—the region doesn't change, and the policy from the original group doesn't carry over.

Since Sub1 is part of MG1, and RG1 is inside Sub1, the User Access Administrator permission applies to RG1 as well. While Contributor alone does not allow role assignment, the User Access Administrator role is specifically designed to allow assigning any RBAC role, including Owner, as long as the user has this role at the appropriate level—which User1 does in this case. Therefore, User1 can assign the Owner role for RG1, even if they are not currently an Owner themselves.

question:
Note: This question is part of a set of related questions that use the same scenario. Each question

proposes a different solution that may or may not satisfy the stated requirement.

You have three Azure subscriptions named Sub1, Sub2, and Sub3, all associated with a single

Microsoft Entra tenant.

The tenant includes a user named User1, a security group named Group1, and a management group

named MG1. User1 is a member of Group1.

Both Sub1 and Sub2 are assigned to MG1.

Sub1 contains a resource group named RG1, and RG1 hosts five Azure Functions.

The following role assignments are configured at the MG1 scope:

• Group1 is assigned the Reader role

• User1 is assigned the User Access Administrator role

Additionally:

• User1 is assigned the Virtual Machine Contributor role on Sub1 and Sub2

• User1 is assigned the Contributor role on RG1

True or False:

"User1 can create a new resource group and deploy a virtual machine to the new group."
explanation: False is the correct answer here. Although User1 has the Virtual Machine Contributor role assigned at the Sub1 and Sub2 subscription levels, and the Contributor role for RG1, they do not have permissions to create a new resource group unless they are granted Owner or Contributor at the subscription level where they want to create that new resource group. The Virtual Machine Contributor role allows managing virtual machines, but does not grant permissions to create resource groups. Additionally, the Contributor role assigned at RG1 only provides permissions within RG1, not at the subscription level needed to create new resource groups. Therefore, User1 cannot create a new resource group, and thus, cannot deploy a VM to a new resource group.

question:
You have an Azure subscription named Subscription1 and an on-premises deployment of Microsoft

System Center Service Manager.

Within Subscription1, there is a virtual machine named VM1.

You must ensure that Service Manager generates an alert whenever the available memory on VM1

drops below 10 percent.

What should you do first?

options.C: Deploy the IT Service Management Connector (ITSM)

explanation: Deploy the IT Service Management Connector (ITSM) is the correct answer here. The IT Service Management Connector (ITSM) allows you to integrate Azure Monitor with IT service management tools such as System Center Service Manager (SCSM). This connector enables alerts from Azure (e.g., when VM1's available memory drops below a threshold) to automatically generate incidents or alerts within Service Manager. Before you can generate alerts or trigger incidents in Service Manager based on Azure metrics, you must first deploy and configure the ITSM connector in Azure. Only then can you map Azure alerts (like memory thresholds) to corresponding actions in Service Manager. Create an automation runbook is incorrect because automation runbooks are used for remediating or performing actions based on alerts, not for integrating with Service Manager directly. Deploy a function app is incorrect as it's generally used for executing custom serverless logic—not necessary in this scenario where a built-in integration exists via ITSM Connector. Create a notification is incorrect because notifications are used to inform users via email or SMS, but not to trigger actions or alerts in Service Manager.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that includes the following resources, all deployed in the East US

region:

• 10 virtual machines

• A key vault named Vault1

• A network security group named NSG1

All virtual machines are protected by using NSG1, which is configured to deny all outbound internet

traffic.

You must allow the virtual machines to access Vault1. The solution must follow the principle of least

privilege and require minimal ongoing administration.

Which destination should you specify in the outbound security rule for NSG1?
explanation: a service tag is the correct answer here. To allow the virtual machines to access Vault1 (which is an Azure Key Vault resource) while keeping outbound internet access blocked, you should configure the NSG outbound rule to allow traffic only to the AzureKeyVault service tag. Service tags represent a group of IP address prefixes for specific Azure services and are automatically maintained by Microsoft, which minimizes administrative effort and adheres to the principle of least privilege. By using the AzureKeyVault service tag, you allow access only to Key Vault endpoints and nothing else on the internet, satisfying both security and operational requirements. an application security group is incorrect because ASGs are used to group VMs and simplify NSG rules within a virtual network, not for allowing access to Azure services like Key Vault. an IP address range is incorrect because allowing access via public IP ranges to Key Vault would require you to manage and update the ranges manually, which increases administrative overhead and violates the principle of least privilege.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the following virtual machines, all deployed in the same

virtual network (VNET1):

• VM-A

◦ OS: Windows Server

◦ Subnet: SubnetA

• VM-B

◦ OS: Windows Server

◦ Subnet: SubnetB

• VM-C

◦ OS: Red Hat Enterprise Linux

◦ Subnet: SubnetC

Each virtual machine's network interface is configured with the following DNS settings:

• VM-A -> No DNS server configured

• VM-B -> 192.168.10.15

• VM-C -> 192.168.10.15

At the virtual network level, custom DNS settings are configured with the following DNS server:

• 193.77.134.10

All virtual machines can successfully reach both DNS servers (192.168.10.15 and 193.77.134.10).

True or False:

"VM-A connects to 193.77.134.10 for DNS queries."
explanation: True is correct because VM-A does not have a custom DNS server configured at the network interface level. In such cases, Azure virtual machines inherit their DNS server settings from the virtual network (VNET) they are connected to. From the information provided, VNET1 is configured with a single custom DNS server: 193.77.134.10. Therefore, VM-A uses 193.77.134.10 for DNS queries. The DNS server 192.168.10.15 is manually configured only for VM-B and VM-C at their respective NIC level and is not part of the VNET-wide configuration. Since VM-A lacks its own DNS override, it relies solely on the VNET1 configuration.

explanation: False is the correct answer because VM-B is explicitly configured with a custom DNS server: 192.168.10.15 on its network interface. You create a service endpoint policy named StoragePolicy01 in the South Central US region. The

policy is configured to allow access to all storage accounts in the subscription.

True or False:

"StoragePolicy01 can be applied to Subnet-C."
explanation: True is the correct answer because Subnet-C is in VNet-US, which is located in the South Central US region, the same region in which the service endpoint policy (StoragePolicy01) was created. For a service endpoint policy to be applied to a subnet: • The subnet must have a matching service endpoint (in this case, Microsoft.Storage). • The subnet and the service endpoint policy must be in the same region. question:
You manage an Azure subscription.

You need to create a custom Azure RBAC role with the following requirements:

• The assigned users must be able to perform all management operations for a virtual

network.

• The permissions must adhere to the principle of least privilege, meaning no unnecessary access

beyond what is required to manage the virtual network.

Which permissions should you specify in the role definition to meet these requirements?
explanation: "Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/*" is the correct answer because it grants permission to perform all actions on virtual networks, including read, write, delete, and other operations such as joining subnets or modifying settings. The asterisk * is a wildcard that encompasses all actions under the Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks resource provider. This meets the requirement that users must be able to perform all actions on a virtual network. "Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/delete" is incorrect because it grants only the ability to delete virtual networks and does not include permissions to read, write, or manage other aspects of the virtual network. "Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/write" is incorrect because it only provides write access (e.g., create or update) but not read or delete access, and therefore does not fulfill the requirement of allowing all actions.

question:
You manage an Azure subscription.

You need to create a custom Azure RBAC role with the following requirements:

• Users must be able to view the configuration settings of a storage account.

• The permissions must adhere to the principle of least privilege, meaning no unnecessary access

beyond what is required to manage the virtual network.

Which permissions should you specify in the role definition to meet these requirements?

"Microsoft.Storage/StorageAccounts/*"
explanation: "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/read" is the correct answer because it grants users read-only access to the configuration and metadata of the storage account (such as properties, settings, keys, and networking configurations), without allowing any modifications or access to the actual data stored in blobs, queues, or files. This fully aligns with the principle of least privilege and the stated requirement to view configuration data only. "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/*" is incorrect because it grants all permissions on the storage account, including write and delete operations, which violates the principle of least privilege. "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/read" is incorrect because it only provides read access to blob data, not to the configuration settings of the storage account itself.

question:
You have an Azure App Service plan named AppServicePlanA that is configured with the Standard

pricing tier.

You need to configure the plan so that it automatically increases its instance count whenever the web

app's CPU utilization exceeds 80 percent.

Which configuration setting should you enable for AppServicePlanA to achieve this behavior?

options.A: Automatic scaling configured in the Scale out settings
options.B: Rule-based scaling configured in the Scale out settings
options.C: Premium P1 selected under the Scale up (App Service plan) settings
options.D: Standard S1 selected under the Scale up (App Service plan) settings
options.E: Manual scaling configured in the Scale out settings

explanation: Rule-based scaling configured in the Scale out settings is the correct answer here. By selecting Rules Based, you can configure specific conditions for automatic scaling, such as when CPU usage exceeds 80 percent. This allows AppServicePlanA to automatically add more instances when the CPU utilization goes above the defined threshold. In this case, a rule can be created to automatically scale out based on CPU performance, which satisfies the requirement. Automatic scaling configured in the Scale out settings is incorrect because it doesn't allow setting specific scaling conditions, such as CPU thresholds. Manual scaling configured in the Scale out settings is incorrect because it requires manual intervention to scale, which does not meet the requirement of automatic scaling when CPU usage exceeds 80 percent. Premium P1 selected under the Scale up (App Service plan) settings and Standard S1 selected under the Scale up (App Service plan) settings are incorrect because these refer to scaling up (increasing the resources of the plan itself), not scaling out (adding more instances) based on a specific condition like CPU usage.

question:
You have an Azure virtual network named VNet1 with the following configuration:

• The IPv4 address space is 172.16.10.0/24

• A subnet named Subnet1 exists within the virtual network

• Subnet1 uses the address range 172.16.10.0/25

Based on this configuration, what is the maximum number of virtual machines that can be deployed and

connected to Subnet1?
explanation: 123 is the correct answer. The subnet 172.16.10.0/25 has a total of 128 IP addresses. However, Azure reserves the first four and the last IP address in every subnet for internal use. Therefore, the available IP addresses for virtual machines are: 128 (total IP addresses) - 5 (reserved addresses) = 123 usable IP addresses. These 123 addresses can be assigned to virtual machines or other resources within the subnet. • 172.16.10.0/25 means the subnet has 128 total IP addresses (2^7 = 128). • Azure reserves five IP addresses in each subnet: • The first IP is the network address. • The second through fourth IP addresses are reserved for Azure services. • The last IP address is reserved for the broadcast address. • Thus, 123 addresses remain available for virtual machines.

question:
Your environment includes an on-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) domain with the

identities listed below:

• User1 is a user account located in OU2.

• User2 is a user account located in OU1.

• Group1 is a global security group that includes User1 and is located in OU1.

You have an Azure subscription that contains a storage account named storage1.

The Azure Files shares in storage1 use AD DS as the identity source, and the default share-level

permissions are configured to allow access for all authenticated users and groups.

You create an Azure Files share named share1 and assign the following roles:

• User2 is assigned the Storage File Data SMB Share Reader role.

• Group1 is assigned the Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor role.

You also have a Microsoft Entra tenant that includes a cloud-only user named User3.

Microsoft Entra Connect is configured to synchronize OU1 from the on-premises AD DS domain to the

Microsoft Entra tenant.

True or False:

"User1 is able to access the data stored in share1."
explanation: True is the correct answer because User1 can access share1 by using AD DS authentication, even though User1 is not synchronized to Microsoft Entra ID. The storage account uses AD DS as the identity source, and default share-level permissions are enabled for all authenticated users and groups. For Azure Files with AD DS authentication, Microsoft states that when a default share-level permission is configured, on-premises AD DS identities do not need to be synchronized to Microsoft Entra ID. The identity only needs to authenticate against the AD DS deployment associated with the storage account. In addition, User1 is a member of Group1 in the on-premises AD DS domain. Group1 is located in OU1, is synchronized to Microsoft Entra ID, and has the Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor role on share1. Microsoft states that for AD DS authentication, non-synchronized users can still access Azure file shares through membership in a synchronized AD DS group. Azure Files reads the group SIDs from the user's Kerberos ticket and applies the matching RBAC role assignments. Therefore, User1 can access the data in share1, assuming the applicable NTFS/file-level permissions do not deny access. Azure Files evaluates both share-level permissions and Windows ACLs, and the most restrictive permission applies.

identities listed below:

True or False:

"User2 can access content in share1."
explanation: True is correct. User2 can access share1 because User2 is located in OU1, and OU1 is synchronized to Microsoft Entra ID. User2 is also explicitly assigned the Storage File Data SMB Share Reader role on share1, which grants read access at the Azure Files share level. Additionally, the question states that the default share-level permissions are configured to allow access for all authenticated users and groups. Therefore, even without the explicit RBAC assignment, User2 could still be allowed at the share level if User2 can authenticate against the associated AD DS domain and the default permission grants sufficient access. However, Azure Files access is controlled by both share-level permissions and NTFS file/directory permissions. Therefore, actual access to the content also depends on the applicable NTFS ACLs. In this question, no restrictive NTFS ACL is mentioned, so User2 can access the content in share1.

question:
You manage two Azure subscriptions, Sub1 and Sub2. Each subscription is linked to a

separate Microsoft Entra tenant.

The environment includes the following virtual networks:

• VNet1 – Located in East US – Associated with Sub1

• VNet2 – Located in East US – Associated with Sub1

• VNet3 – Located in West US – Associated with Sub1

• VNet4 – Located in East US – Associated with Sub2

• VNet5 – Located in Central US – Associated with Sub2

You want to establish virtual network peering from VNet1.

Which of the listed virtual networks are eligible to be peered with VNet1?
explanation: VNet1 can peer with VNet2, VNet3, VNet4, and VNet5 because global virtual network peering allows you to peer virtual networks across different regions and subscriptions, even when they are linked to different Microsoft Entra tenants. • VNet2: Same region (East US), same subscription (Sub1). • VNet3: Different region (West US), same subscription (Sub1). • VNet4: Same region (East US), different subscription (Sub2). • VNet5: Different region (Central US), different subscription (Sub2). With global VNet peering, you can enable communication between virtual networks in different regions and subscriptions, as long as the necessary permissions are configured.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that includes a storage account named storage1.

You want to restrict access to storage1 so that it is reachable only from specific networks and from your

home office. The approach must require the least amount of ongoing administrative effort.

What is the first configuration change you should make for storage1?

options.A: Create a private endpoint for the storage account.
options.B: Update the public network access configuration for the storage account.
options.C: Configure the storage account to use internet-based routing.
options.D: Change the role-based access control (IAM) settings.

explanation: Update the public network access configuration for the storage account is the correct answer here. To allow access to storage1 from selected networks and your home office while minimizing administrative effort, you should first modify the Public network access settings. By selecting the option to allow access only from selected virtual networks and IP addresses, you can define specific networks and IP addresses, such as your home office's public IP address, without needing to configure more complex solutions like private endpoints. Create a private endpoint for the storage account is incorrect because private endpoints require additional setup and would only allow access through a private network, not minimizing administrative effort. Configure the storage account to use internet-based routing is incorrect because this would open the storage account to access from the internet, which doesn't fulfill the requirement of limiting access to selected networks and your home office. Change the role-based access control (IAM) settings is incorrect because IAM controls user and group permissions for accessing resources but does not control network access.

question:
An Azure subscription contains three Azure Container Registry (ACR) instances. Each registry is

configured with a different pricing tier:

• ContReg2 – Service tier: Standard

• ContReg3 – Service tier: Basic

You plan to use Azure Container Registry (ACR) Tasks and also require support for private endpoint

connections.

Which of the listed container registries can be used to run ACR Tasks?
explanation: ContReg1, ContReg2, and ContReg3 is the correct answer here. ACR Tasks are supported in all service tiers: Basic, Standard, and Premium. While there are performance and feature differences across the tiers (such as the number of concurrent tasks or webhook triggers), ACR Tasks functionality is available in all three tiers, including Basic.

question:
You have an Azure container registry named contoso2023 as shown below.

You want to configure contoso2023 so that it uses a dedicated data endpoint for data operations.

Which two configuration settings must you enable or modify on contoso2023 to meet this requirement?
explanation: To enable contoso2023 to use a dedicated data endpoint, you need to configure the following two settings: Properties: This is where you can enable and configure the dedicated data endpoint for your Azure container registry. From this blade, you must first change the pricing plan from Standard to Premium. This setting is crucial for routing all data plane operations through a dedicated endpoint. Networking: After the registry is upgraded to Premium, you must go to Networking and enable the dedicated data endpoint setting. Dedicated data endpoints provide registry-specific data endpoint URLs, such as <registry-name>.<region>.data.azurecr.io, for data operations. question:
You have a Microsoft Entra tenant named contoso.com.

You work with an external organization that uses the domain fabrikam.com.

You plan to invite external users from fabrikam.com into the contoso.com tenant.

You must ensure that invitations can be sent exclusively to users from fabrikam.com and not to users

from any other external domains.

What configuration should you perform in the Microsoft Entra admin center?

options.A: From Cross-tenant access settings, configure the Tenant restrictions settings.
options.B: From Cross-tenant access settings, configure the Microsoft cloud settings.
options.C: From External collaboration settings, configure the Guest user access restrictions settings.
options.D: From External collaboration settings, configure the Collaboration restrictions settings.

explanation: From External collaboration settings, configure the Collaboration restrictions settings is the correct answer. In Microsoft Entra, you can restrict who can be invited as a guest by configuring Collaboration restrictions. By specifying the allowed domains, such as fabrikam.com, you can ensure that invitations can only be sent to users from that domain. From Cross-tenant access settings, configure the Tenant restrictions settings is incorrect because tenant restrictions are used to control which tenants users can access, not to restrict guest invitations. From Cross-tenant access settings, configure the Microsoft cloud settings is incorrect because these settings are used for managing cross-tenant access policies between Microsoft cloud environments, not for restricting guest user invitations. From External collaboration settings, configure the Guest user access restrictions settings is incorrect because this setting controls what guest users can do once they are in your tenant, not who can be invited.

chapter: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
question:
You have an Azure subscription that includes three virtual machines named VM1, VM2, and VM3. All

three virtual machines are deployed in the same availability set called AVSet1.

You want to resize VM1 to a larger virtual machine size. However, the target size is currently not

available.

What action should you take first?

options.A: Create a proximity placement group and associate it with the virtual machines.
options.C: Convert AvSet1 into a managed availability set.

explanation: Deallocate VM1 is the correct answer here. When a specific virtual machine size is unavailable for a VM that is part of an availability set (like AVSet1), the first step is to deallocate the virtual machine. Deallocating the VM releases the hardware allocation, potentially freeing up capacity for the new VM size. Once the VM is deallocated, you can attempt to resize it. Create a proximity placement group and associate it with the virtual machines is incorrect because proximity placement groups are used to ensure low-latency placement of VMs but have no direct impact on resizing availability. Convert AVSet1 into a managed availability set is incorrect because the availability set is already managed by default when using managed disks, and this action wouldn't resolve the size availability issue. Power off VM2 and VM3 is incorrect because shutting down the other VMs in the availability set does not affect the resizing of VM1.

question:
An Azure subscription contains the following resources:

• VM1 – Virtual machine

• VNet1 – Virtual network

• NIC1 – Network interface

• LB1 – Load balancer

• VPN1 – Virtual network gateway

You create a new public IP address named IP1.

Which two of the listed resources can be linked to IP1?
explanation: LB1 (Load balancer) and NIC1 (Network interface) are the correct answers. Public IP addresses can be associated with a load balancer or a network interface to enable external communication with resources like virtual machines or services behind the load balancer. • LB1: A public IP can be associated with a load balancer to distribute incoming traffic across multiple backend resources, such as virtual machines. • NIC1: A public IP can also be associated with a network interface, allowing a virtual machine to have direct access to the internet. VM1 is incorrect because public IP addresses are associated with network interfaces (like NIC1) rather than directly with virtual machines. VPN1 is incorrect because virtual network gateways use their own public IPs but are not directly associated with manually created public IPs. VNet1 is incorrect because virtual networks themselves do not have public IP addresses directly associated with them.

question:
You have an Azure subscription with two virtual networks, VNet1 and VNet2, that are peered with each

other.

VNet1 includes a VPN gateway that is configured to use static routing.

The on-premises network has a VPN connection that uses the VPN gateway of VNet1.

You need to enable users from the on-premises network to access a virtual machine hosted in VNet2.

The solution must be cost-effective.

Which connectivity approach should you implement?

options.A: Deploy Azure Firewall and route traffic through its private IP address
options.B: Use service chaining together with user-defined routes (UDRs)
options.D: Provision an ExpressRoute circuit connected to VNet2

explanation: Use service chaining together with user-defined routes (UDRs) is the correct answer. By using service chaining and configuring user-defined routes (UDRs), you can route traffic from the on-premises network, through the VPN gateway on VNet1, to VNet2. This setup leverages the existing peering between VNet1 and VNet2 without requiring additional costly infrastructure like Azure Firewall or ExpressRoute, thereby minimizing costs. UDRs will ensure that the traffic is directed through the correct paths. Deploy Azure Firewall and route traffic through its private IP address is incorrect because while it could provide routing and security, it is more costly than using UDRs and is not necessary for this scenario. Deploy an Azure Application Gateway is incorrect because this is primarily used for managing and load balancing web traffic, not for routing network traffic between VNets or from on-premises networks. Provision an ExpressRoute circuit connected to VNet2 is incorrect because ExpressRoute is a high- cost solution that provides private connectivity between on-premises and Azure, which is not required since you already have a VPN gateway in place for the on-premises connection.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that contains a storage account named storage1.

You want to make sure that the access keys for storage1 are rotated automatically.

Which configuration should you set up?
explanation: Configure an Azure Key Vault is the correct answer. To ensure that the access keys for storage1 rotate automatically, you should store the keys in Azure Key Vault and enable key rotation policies. Key Vault allows for the secure storage of secrets, including storage account access keys, and provides the ability to configure automatic key rotation. Configure a backup vault and Configure a Recovery Services vault are incorrect because these are used for backing up data and managing disaster recovery, not for rotating access keys. Configure redundancy settings for storage1 is incorrect because this deals with the replication of storage data across different locations for high availability, not key management. Configure lifecycle management for storage1 is incorrect because this manages data retention policies, not access key rotation.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that includes a storage account named storage1, which stores blob

data.

You must assign a role to a user named User1 so that the user can access the blob data in storage1.

The role assignment must support Azure role assignment conditions.

Which two roles are suitable for assigning to User1?
explanation: Storage Blob Data Contributor is the correct answer because this role allows the user to read, write, and delete blob data within a storage account. This role supports conditions, which can help control access based on specific criteria like time, IP address, or other factors. Storage Blob Data Owner is the correct answer because this role grants full control over blob data, including setting access policies and modifying blob content. It also supports conditions for access. Owner is incorrect because while this role gives full administrative access to the storage account, it does not allow direct blob data access, nor does it support conditions for blob-level data access. Storage Account Contributor is incorrect because it grants management access to the storage account but does not provide direct access to blob data. Storage Account Backup Contributor is incorrect because this role is designed for backup and recovery operations but doesn't provide direct access to blob data. Storage Blob Delegator is incorrect because this role is used to delegate access through OAuth 2.0 on behalf of a user or service and is not intended for direct blob data access.

question:
You have a Microsoft Entra tenant.

You plan to import a large number of user accounts at once.

You must ensure that newly imported users are automatically added to a specific group based on the

value of their department attribute. The solution should require minimal ongoing administrative effort.

Which two actions should you take?

options.A: Create groups that use the Assigned membership type.
options.B: Create an Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template.
options.C: Create groups that use the Dynamic User membership type.
options.D: Write a PowerShell script that parses an import file.
options.E: Create an XML file that contains user information and the appropriate attributes.
options.F: Create a CSV file that contains user information and the appropriate attributes.

explanation: Create groups that use the Dynamic User membership type is the correct answer because dynamic membership rules allow users to be automatically added to groups based on specific attributes, such as department. This minimizes administrative effort since the users will be automatically placed into the correct group based on their department attribute without manual intervention. Create a CSV file that contains user information and the appropriate attributes is the correct answer because CSV is the supported format for bulk importing users into Microsoft Entra. The CSV file will contain the necessary user information, including department attributes, which are used to assign users to the appropriate dynamic groups. Create groups that use the Assigned membership type is incorrect because assigned groups require manual assignment of users, which does not minimize administrative effort. Create an Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template is incorrect because ARM templates are used to deploy Azure resources, not for user or group management. Write a PowerShell script that parses an import file is incorrect because while it can be used, it would increase administrative effort, which is against the goal of minimizing effort. Create an XML file that contains user information and the appropriate attributes is incorrect because CSV is the recommended format for bulk user import, not XML.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure Container Registry named RegistryProd01,

which is currently configured with the Standard pricing tier.

You need to enable support for geo-replication for RegistryProd01.

What is the first step you should perform on RegistryProd01 to meet this requirement?

options.A: Enable the admin user for the registry.
options.B: Create a scope map for the registry.
options.E: Change the registry to a higher SKU tier.

explanation: Change the registry to a higher SKU tier is the correct answer here. Geo-replication in Azure Container Registry is only supported in the Premium SKU. Since RegistryProd01 is currently using the Standard SKU, the first step to enable geo-replication is to upgrade the SKU to Premium. Once the SKU is upgraded, you can configure geo-replication across multiple regions. Enable the admin user for the registry is incorrect because this is related to authentication and does not enable geo-replication. Create a scope map for the registry is incorrect because scope maps are used for defining permissions for tokens, not for geo-replication. Configure an automation task is incorrect because automation tasks are used for building and pushing images, not for geo-replication. Define a cache rule is incorrect because cache rules are unrelated to geo-replication.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that includes a storage account named storage1 which contains a blob

used to store images.

Access to storage1 is provided to clients by using a shared access signature (SAS).

You want users to see a warning whenever they create a SAS with an expiration period longer than

seven days.

What configuration should you apply to the storage account?

options.A: Enable a read-only resource lock on the storage account.
options.B: Create and configure an alert rule.
options.D: Set Allow recommended upper limit for shared access signature (SAS) expiry interval to

explanation: Set Allow recommended upper limit for shared access signature (SAS) expiry interval to Enabled is the correct answer. By enabling this setting, Azure will enforce a recommended upper limit for SAS token expiry (in this case, seven days). Users will receive a warning if they try to create a SAS token that exceeds the defined limit, helping to maintain secure access practices. Enable a read-only resource lock on the storage account is incorrect because locks are used to prevent modification or deletion of resources, not for configuring SAS expiry limits. Create and configure an alert rule is incorrect because alert rules are used for monitoring and alerting on events, but do not directly enforce or warn about SAS expiry time. Add a lifecycle management policy is incorrect because lifecycle management is used to manage blob storage tiers and deletion policies, not SAS expiry intervals.

question:
You have an Azure subscription linked to a hybrid Microsoft Entra tenant. The tenant includes the users

listed below:

• User1: Not enabled for on-premises synchronization

• User2: Enabled for on-premises synchronization

You create the following Azure Files shares:

• share1 in storage account contoso2025

• share2 in storage account contoso2025

• share3 in storage account contoso2026

You configure identity-based access for contoso2025 by enabling Active Directory Domain Services

(AD DS) as the identity source and setting the default share-level permissions to allow access for all

authenticated users and groups.

True or False:

"User1 can access the content in share1."
explanation: False is correct because User1 does not have on-premises synchronization enabled, as indicated. According to the identity-based access configuration shown in the exhibit, only users synchronized from on-premises AD DS or those with hybrid identities can access the file shares. User1 is not synced from an on-premises AD DS environment and is therefore not eligible for access to share1, despite the permissions being enabled for authenticated users.

question:
A Microsoft Entra tenant contains the following users:

◦ Member of: Group1

◦ Assigned license: Microsoft Entra ID P2

◦ Member of: Group2

• User3

◦ Assigned license: None

The tenant also contains the following groups and group relationships:

• Group1

◦ Member of: No groups

◦ Assigned license: None

• Group2

◦ Member of: Group3

◦ Assigned license: Microsoft Entra ID P2

• Group3

◦ Member of: Group4

◦ Assigned license: None

• Group4

◦ Member of: No groups

◦ Assigned license: Microsoft Entra ID P2

Based on the tenant configuration shown above, which users are eligible to be deleted from Microsoft

Entra ID?
explanation: User1, User2, User3, and User4 can all be deleted. In Microsoft Entra ID, users can be deleted regardless of whether they have licenses assigned directly or through group membership. When a user is deleted, any licenses assigned to them will be freed for reassignment.

question:

◦ Assigned license: Microsoft Entra ID P2

Based on the tenant configuration shown above, which groups are eligible to be deleted from Microsoft

explanation: Group1 and Group3 only is the correct answer because both groups do not have any licenses directly assigned to them. According to Microsoft Entra documentation, a group cannot be deleted if it has licenses directly assigned. Group1 and Group3 meet the criteria for deletion: Group1 has no assigned license, and Group3 is only a member of another group but does not itself have any license directly assigned. Group4 only is incorrect because Group4 has a Microsoft Entra ID P2 license assigned directly, which prevents it from being deleted until the license is removed. Group1 only is incorrect because while Group1 can be deleted, Group3 can also be deleted, so this answer is incomplete. question:

You plan to configure Azure Backup reports for RSVault1.

While configuring diagnostic settings for the AzureBackupReports log category, you must choose a

storage account as the destination.

Which storage accounts are eligible to store the Azure Backup reports for RSVault1?
explanation: dataStore3 only is correct because Azure Backup requires that the storage account used for diagnostic settings (like Azure Backup reports) be in the same region as the Recovery Services vault (RSVault1). Since RSVault1 is in the West Europe region, only dataStore3, located in West Europe, meets this requirement. dataStore1 only is incorrect because dataStore1 is in the East US region, which does not match the West Europe region of Vault1. dataStore2 only is incorrect because dataStore2 is in the West US region, which also does not match the West Europe region of Vault1. dataStore1, dataStore2, and dataStore3 is incorrect because only dataStore3 is in the same region as Vault1. dataStore1 and dataStore2 are in East US and West US, respectively, and therefore cannot be used.

Which Log Analytics workspaces can you use for the Azure Backup reports of RSVault1?
explanation: LogWorkspace1, LogWorkspace2, and LogWorkspace3 is correct because, as per the documentation, the location of the Log Analytics workspace does not need to match the location of the Recovery Services vault. Therefore, all three workspaces LogWorkspace1, LogWorkspace2, and LogWorkspace3, can be used to store the Azure Backup reports for Vault1.

question:
You have an on-premises network and an Azure subscription that includes three peered virtual

networks named VNET1, VNET2, and VNET3. All three virtual networks are connected to the on-

premises network.

The subscription contains the following virtual machines:

• VM1 and VM2, located in West US and connected to VNET1

• VM3, located in West US and connected to VNET2

• VM4, located in Central US and connected to VNET3

You want to monitor network connectivity between the virtual machines and the on-premises network by

using Connection Monitor.

What is the minimum number of Connection Monitor instances that you must deploy?
explanation: 2 is correct because Azure Network Watcher's Connection Monitor requires that the source virtual machine and the Connection Monitor instance reside in the same Azure region. In the table: • VM1, VM2, and VM3 are in the West US region. • VM4 is in the Central US region. You will need: 1. One Connection Monitor in West US to monitor VM1, VM2, and VM3's connectivity to the on- premises network. 2. One Connection Monitor in Central US to monitor VM4's connectivity to the on-premises network. You cannot use a single connection monitor to monitor VMs across regions, hence two are required.

question:
An Azure subscription contains two virtual machines with the following configurations:

• VM1

◦ Operating system: Windows Server 2019

◦ Connected to: Subnet1

• VM2

◦ Operating system: Windows Server 2019

◦ Connected to: Subnet2

Both VM1 and VM2 have public IP addresses, and inbound Remote Desktop (RDP) access is enabled

on each virtual machine.

Subnet1 and Subnet2 belong to the same virtual network named VNET1.

The subscription contains two network security groups (NSGs):

• NSG1 contains only the default security rules.

• NSG2 contains the default rules and an additional inbound rule with the following configuration:

◦ Priority: 100

◦ Name: Rule1

◦ Protocol: TCP

◦ Port: 3389

◦ Source: Any

◦ Destination: Any

◦ Action: Allow

NSG1 is associated with Subnet1, and NSG2 is associated with the network interface of VM2.

True or False:

"You can connect to VM1 from the internet using Remote Desktop."
explanation: False is correct because VM1 is associated with NSG1, which only has the default rules. By default, NSGs deny inbound traffic from the internet unless there is an explicit rule to allow it. Since NSG1 does not have any custom rule allowing inbound Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) traffic on port 3389 from the internet, VM1 cannot be accessed via RDP from the internet.

question:
You have an Azure virtual network named VNet1, as shown in the exhibit.

VNet1 has an address space of 10.2.0.0/16, and currently no devices are connected to it.

You plan to create a virtual network peering between VNet1 and another virtual network named VNet2.

VNet2 also uses the address space 10.2.0.0/16.

You need to establish the peering between the two virtual networks.

What action should you perform first?

options.A: Add a gateway subnet to VNet1.
options.B: Create a subnet on VNet1 and VNet2.
options.C: Modify the address space of VNet1.
options.D: Configure a service endpoint on VNet2.

explanation: Modify the address space of VNet1 is correct because the address spaces of two virtual networks being peered must not overlap. In this case, both VNet1 and VNet2 have the address space 10.2.0.0/16, which causes an overlap and prevents peering. To enable peering, you would first need to modify the address space of VNet1 to a non-overlapping range. Add a gateway subnet to VNet1 is incorrect because a gateway subnet is only required for VPN Gateway connections, not for simple VNet peering. Create a subnet on VNet1 and VNet2 is incorrect because the presence of subnets is not a requirement for VNet peering. The issue here is the overlapping address space, which must be resolved first. Configure a service endpoint on VNet2 is incorrect because service endpoints are used to secure access to Azure services and are not related to VNet peering configuration.

question:
You have an Azure subscription named ProductionSub.

You are designing a multi-tier application with the following architecture:

• Web tier

◦ Internet-facing: Yes

◦ Number of virtual machines: 10

• Application/Business tier

◦ Internet-facing: No

◦ Number of virtual machines: 100

• Database tier (SQL Server)

◦ Internet-facing: No

◦ Number of virtual machines: 5

You must recommend a networking solution that ensures traffic from the web tier to the application tier

is evenly distributed across all virtual machines in the application tier.

Which Azure resource should you recommend to meet this requirement?

options.A: an application gateway that uses the Standard tier
options.B: an application gateway that uses the WAF tier

explanation: An internal load balancer is correct because an internal load balancer in Azure is designed to distribute network traffic within a virtual network (VNet) across virtual machines (VMs) without exposing them to the internet. In this scenario, it can be used to balance the load between the front-end web servers and the business logic tier, ensuring that traffic spreads equally across the VMs in the business logic tier. Since the business logic tier is not accessible from the internet, an internal load balancer is the appropriate solution. An application gateway that uses the Standard tier is incorrect because an application gateway is primarily designed for web traffic (HTTP/HTTPS) and is typically used in internet-facing scenarios or for application layer load balancing, which is not specified here. An application gateway that uses the WAF tier is incorrect for the same reason as above. Additionally, the WAF tier is designed to protect applications from web vulnerabilities, which is unnecessary for internal load balancing between tiers in this setup. A network security group (NSG) is incorrect because NSGs are used for filtering network traffic based on security rules and do not provide load balancing capabilities. A public load balancer is incorrect because it is used to distribute traffic from the internet to VMs within a VNet. Since the business logic tier is not accessible from the internet, a public load balancer is not suitable.

question:
You have an Azure subscription named ProductionSub.

You are designing a multi-tier application with the following architecture:

• Web tier

◦ Internet-facing: Yes

◦ Number of virtual machines: 10

• Application/Business tier

◦ Internet-facing: No

◦ Number of virtual machines: 100

• Database tier (SQL Server)

◦ Internet-facing: No

◦ Number of virtual machines: 5

You must recommend a networking solution that protects the web tier from SQL injection attacks

originating from the internet.

Which Azure resource should you recommend to meet this requirement?

options.A: an application gateway that uses the Standard tier
options.B: an application gateway that uses the WAF tier

explanation: An application gateway that uses the WAF tier is correct because the Web Application Firewall (WAF) tier of Azure Application Gateway provides built-in protection against common web vulnerabilities, including SQL injection attacks. By placing an application gateway with WAF in front of the web servers, you can protect them from SQL injection and other security threats. An application gateway that uses the Standard tier is incorrect because the Standard tier does not include WAF functionality, which is required to protect against SQL injection. An internal load balancer is incorrect because load balancers are used to distribute network traffic and do not offer protection against SQL injection or other web vulnerabilities. A network security group (NSG) is incorrect because NSGs control access through rules but do not provide protection against specific types of attacks like SQL injection. A public load balancer is incorrect because, like an internal load balancer, it only distributes traffic and does not protect against web vulnerabilities.

question:
You have a virtual network named VNet1 with an address space of 10.2.0.0/16 and a single subnet

configured as 10.2.0.0/24.

You plan to deploy a virtual machine in VNet1 and assign it an IP address from the 192.168.1.0/24

address range.

Before the virtual machine can receive an IP address from 192.168.1.0/24, what must you do first?
explanation: Add an address space is correct because the existing address space of VNet1 is configured as 10.2.0.0/16. To allow virtual machines on VNet1 to receive an IP address from 192.168.1.0/24, you must first add this new address space to VNet1. Azure virtual networks support multiple address spaces, but they must be added explicitly. Add a network interface is incorrect because a network interface allows a VM to connect to a subnet but does not affect the IP range available within the virtual network. Add a subnet is incorrect because adding a new subnet would require an available address space in the 192.168.1.0/24 range, which is not currently defined within VNet1. Delete a subnet is incorrect because deleting a subnet will not allow adding the desired IP range. Delete an address space is incorrect because the action required is to add a new address space, not remove an existing one.

question:
You have a virtual network named VNet1 with an address space of 10.2.0.0/16 and a single subnet

configured as 10.2.0.0/24.

Based on the current address space and subnet configuration, a virtual machine deployed in VNet1

must be assigned an IP address from the 10.2.1.0/24 range.

What must you do before the virtual machine can receive an IP address from this range?
explanation: Add a subnet is correct because the current address space for VNet1 is 10.2.0.0/16, which already includes the 10.2.1.0/24 range. However, there is only one existing subnet (default) configured with the 10.2.0.0/24 address prefix. To assign IP addresses from 10.2.1.0/24, you would need to create a new subnet using this address range within the existing address space. Add a network interface is incorrect because a network interface allows a VM to connect to a subnet but does not create a new address range or subnet. Add an address space is incorrect because 10.2.1.0/24 is already part of the existing 10.2.0.0/16 address space, so adding a new address space is unnecessary. Delete a subnet is incorrect because removing an existing subnet does not help in assigning a new IP range. Delete an address space is incorrect because deleting an address space would reduce the IP range available, which is not required here.

question:
An Azure subscription is associated with a Microsoft Entra tenant named contoso.com. The tenant is

synchronized with an on-premises Active Directory domain.

The domain includes the following users and assigned roles:

• SecAdmin1 – Role: Security Administrator

• BillAdmin1 – Role: Billing Administrator

• User1 – Role: Reports Reader

Self-service password reset (SSPR) is enabled for all users and configured with the following settings:

• Two authentication methods are required to reset a password.

• Available authentication methods are Mobile phone and Security questions.

• Users must register three security questions.

• Users must correctly answer three security questions during password reset.

The following security questions are configured:

• What is your favorite food?

• In what city was your first job?

• What was the name of your first pet?

True or False:

"During a self-service password reset, SecAdmin1 must answer the security question 'In what city was

your first job?'"
explanation: False is correct because, although self-service password reset (SSPR) is enabled for all users, the regular SSPR policy does not apply to users in administrative roles, such as Security Administrator. Administrators must go through a two-gate policy to reset their password, which differs from the standard SSPR process configured for non-admin users. Since SecAdmin1 is in an administrative role, they are excluded from using security questions and instead must follow the enhanced SSPR process that applies to Microsoft Entra ID administrators. Additionally, SSPR is enabled by default for admin roles.

synchronized with an on-premises Active Directory domain.

The domain includes the following users and assigned roles:

• User1 – Role: Reports Reader

Self-service password reset (SSPR) is enabled for all users and configured with the following settings:

• Users must register three security questions.

• In what city was your first job?

• What was the name of your first pet?

True or False:

"During a self-service password reset, BillAdmin1 must answer the security question 'What is your

favorite food?'"
explanation: False is correct because BillAdmin1 has been assigned the Billing Administrator role, which falls under the category of administrative roles in Microsoft Entra. By default, Azure applies a two-gate password reset policy for all administrator accounts. This two-gate policy requires two pieces of authentication data, such as an email address, authenticator app, or phone number, and does not permit the use of security questions for administrators. Therefore, BillAdmin1 would not be prompted to answer a security question, such as "What is your favorite food?" during the password reset process.
