question:
You have three Azure storage accounts configured as follows:

• storage1 — General-purpose v2 (StorageV2), Standard performance, Locally-redundant storage

(LRS), Cool tier

• storage2 — General-purpose v2 (StorageV2), Standard performance, Read-access geo-redundant

storage (RA-GRS), Hot tier

• storage3 — BlobStorage, Premium performance, Locally-redundant storage (LRS), Hot tier

You must identify which storage account can be changed to use zone-redundant storage

(ZRS) replication.

Which storage account meets this requirement?
explanation: storage1 only is correct because it is an LRS account that can directly be converted to a ZRS account. storage2 only is incorrect because RA-GRS account cannot be directly converted to ZRS. However, it can be converted to LRS and then finally converted to ZRS. So technically, both Storage1 and Storage2 accounts can be converted to ZRS, but since we do not have "Storage1 and Storage2 only" as an option in the question, we are assuming it to be asking about direct conversion only. storage3 is incorrect because BlobStorage accounts are not eligible for ZRS replication, regardless of their performance or replication settings. storage2 and storage3 only is incorrect answer here. Storage2 account is RA-GRS which cannot be converted to ZRS directly. Storage3 being a BlobStorage account is not supported for ZRS replication. storage1, storage2, and storage3 are incorrect because only storage1 meets the criteria for direct conversion to ZRS.

question:
You have a registered DNS domain named apexcore.com. You then create a public Azure DNS zone

with the same name (apexcore.com).

You must ensure that any DNS records added to this Azure DNS zone can be successfully resolved by

clients on the public internet.

What action should you take?

options.A: Update the SOA record in the DNS domain registrar.
options.B: Create the SOA record in apexcore.com.
options.C: Update the NS records in the DNS domain registrar.

explanation: Update the NS records in the DNS domain registrar is the correct answer here. To ensure that records created in the apexcore.com Azure DNS zone are resolvable from the internet, you need to update the NS (Name Server) records in your DNS domain registrar. These records should point to the Azure DNS name servers associated with the apexcore.com zone in Azure. This change directs external DNS queries for apexcore.com to Azure DNS, allowing them to be resolved by the public Azure DNS servers. Update the SOA record in the DNS domain registrar is incorrect because the SOA (Start of Authority) record is managed by Azure DNS, and you do not need to modify it in the domain registrar to enable public resolution. Create the SOA record in apexcore.com is incorrect because the SOA record is automatically created and managed by Azure DNS for the zone. No manual action is needed for this record to enable internet resolvability. Create NS records in apexcore.com is incorrect because NS records within the Azure DNS zone are already created automatically. The critical step is to update the NS records at the DNS domain registrar, not within Azure DNS.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that includes a virtual network named VNet1. VNet1 is connected to

two separate on-premises datacenters by using two ExpressRoute circuits.

You need to build a dashboard that provides in-depth network metrics and a graphical view of the

network topology.

Which Azure service should you use?
explanation: Azure Monitor Network Insights is the correct answer here. Azure Monitor Network Insights provides a comprehensive view of your network's health and performance. It includes detailed metrics, visualizations, and insights into the network topology, making it ideal for monitoring complex environments like the one described with multiple ExpressRoute circuits. Azure Virtual Network Watcher is incorrect because, while it offers some monitoring and diagnostic tools for network resources, it does not provide an all-encompassing dashboard or a visual representation of network topology as effectively as Network Insights. A Data Collection Rule (DCR) is incorrect because DCRs are primarily used to define data collection and ingestion rules for Azure Monitor. They do not provide a visual representation of network topology or a network-specific dashboard. Log Analytics is incorrect because it is a tool for querying and analyzing logs. While you can use Log Analytics to query network data, it does not provide a pre-built dashboard or topology visualization as Network Insights does.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that includes the resources mentioned below:

• A virtual network named VNet1

• A subnet named Subnet1, which is part of VNet1

• Two virtual machines, VM1 and VM2, both deployed to Subnet1

VM1 and VM2 were created from the same deployment template and host line-of-business

applications.

You configure a network security group (NSG) as shown in the exhibit.

You need to ensure that users on VM1 and VM2 are unable to browse websites on the internet by

using TCP port 80.

What should you do?

options.A: Modify the DenyWebSites outbound security rule.
options.B: Update the Port_80 inbound security rule.
options.C: Associate the network security group with Subnet1.
options.D: Remove the network security group association from a network interface.

explanation: Associate the network security group with Subnet1 is the correct answer here. The question specifies the need to prevent users of VM1 and VM2 from accessing websites on the Internet over TCP port 80. In the exhibit, there is an outbound rule, DenyWebSites, configured to block traffic on TCP port 80. However, if you look at the "Associated with" section in the top right corner of the exhibit, it shows "0 subnets, 0 network interfaces", meaning this NSG is not currently associated with any subnet or network interface. To apply this restriction to VM1 and VM2, which are located in Subnet1, it is necessary to associate the NSG with Subnet1. By doing so, the NSG rules, including the DenyWebSites rule, will take effect, blocking outbound access to websites on TCP port 80 for both VM1 and VM2. Therefore, Associate the NSG to Subnet1 is the correct choice here. Modify the DenyWebSites outbound security rule is incorrect because modifying the rule itself won't make any difference if the NSG is not associated with Subnet1 or the network interfaces of VM1 and VM2. Update the Port_80 inbound security rule is incorrect because this rule manages inbound traffic on port 80, which is unrelated to the requirement to restrict outbound web access. Remove the network security group association from a network interface is incorrect because there is no existing association to remove, as indicated by the "0 subnets, 0 network interfaces" status.

question:
You have an Azure virtual machine named VM1. You use Azure Backup to create a backup

of VM1 called Backup1.

After Backup1 is created, you make the following changes to VM1:

• Change the virtual machine size.

• Copy a file named Budget.xls into a folder named Data.

• Reset the password for the built-in administrator account.

• Attach an additional data disk to the virtual machine.

An administrator then restores VM1 from Backup1 by using the Replace existing restore option.

You need to ensure that all the changes made after the backup are present on VM1 again.

Which action must you perform again?

options.B: Copy Budget.xls into the Data folder.
options.D: Reset the password for the built-in administrator account.

explanation: Copy Budget.xls into the Data folder is correct because the Replace existing restore option restores the virtual machine disks from the selected recovery point. Any changes made to the contents of the disks after Backup1 was created are reverted. Since the Budget.xls file was copied into the Data folder after the backup was taken, it will not exist after the restore and must be copied again. Attach an additional data disk is incorrect because attaching a data disk is a configuration change to the Azure virtual machine resource itself. The Replace existing restore operation primarily restores the VM disks from the backup recovery point and does not necessarily remove VM-level configuration changes such as attached disk references. Change the size of VM1 is incorrect because the VM size is a property of the Azure virtual machine resource and is not part of the disk contents restored from the recovery point. Restoring the VM disks does not typically revert the VM size configuration. Reset the password for the built-in administrator account is incorrect because password reset operations are commonly managed through VM extensions and VM resource configuration rather than through the restored disk contents alone. The Replace existing operation does not necessarily revert these VM-level settings.

question:
You have an Azure subscription named Subscription1 that contains a resource group with the

following characteristics:

• Name: RG1

• Region: West US

• Tags: "tag1": "value1"

You assign an Azure Policy named Policy1 at the Subscription1 scope with these settings:

• Exclusions: None

• Policy definition: Append a tag and its value to resources

• Assignment name: Policy1

• Parameters:

◦ Tag name: tag2

◦ Tag value: value2

After assigning Policy1, you create a storage account with the following properties:

• Name: storage1

• Region: West US

• Resource group: RG1

• Tags: "tag3": "value3"

Which tags are applied to RG1?
explanation: "tag1" : "value1" only is the correct answer here. The policy definition "Append a tag and its value to resources" is configured to apply to resources within Subscription1, not to the resource group RG1 itself. This policy assignment means that any new resources created under Subscription1 will have the specified tag2 : value2 appended if they do not already have this tag. However, it does not apply the tag to the resource group where the resources are created. Therefore, RG1 retains only the original tag, "tag1" : "value1". It should also be noted here that "Subscription" and "Policy1" are created at the initial stage itself and therefore the created policy would apply to the resource group – namely "RG1" within this subscription. "tag2" : "value2" only is incorrect because Policy1 does not add tag2 : value2 to the resource group itself, only to resources created within the scope of Subscription1. "tag1" : "value1" and "tag2" : "value2" is incorrect because, as explained, Policy1 does not alter tags on the resource group RG1 directly. It only affects newly created resources within Subscription1.

question:

◦ Tag value: value2

After assigning Policy1, you create a storage account with the following properties:

• Name: storage1

• Region: West US

• Resource group: RG1

• Tags: "tag3": "value3"

Which tags are assigned to storage1?

"tag3" : "value3" only
explanation: "tag2" : "value2" and "tag3" : "value3" only is the correct answer here. Tags are not inherited automatically from a resource group or subscription to the resources within them. However, in this case, Policy1 was applied to Subscription1 with the definition to append a specific tag to all new resources created in this subscription. The policy was configured with Exclusions: None and parameters Tag name: "tag2" and Tag value: "value2". This means that all resources created after this policy assignment will automatically have "tag2" : "value2" appended. When storage1 was created in RG1 after the policy was assigned, it had "tag3" : "value3" specified. Since Policy1 was already in effect, "tag2" : "value2" was appended to storage1 due to the policy, resulting in storage1 having the tags "tag2" : "value2" and "tag3" : "value3" only. "tag3" : "value3" only is incorrect because the policy enforces "tag2" : "value2" on all new resources in the subscription. "tag1" : "value1" and "tag3" : "value3" only is incorrect because "tag1" : "value1" is assigned only to RG1 and does not get inherited by resources within the group. "tag1" : "value1", "tag2" : "value2", and "tag3" : "value3" is incorrect because storage1 does not inherit "tag1" : "value1" from RG1.

question:

and security setting.

licensing.

To which groups can you assign a license?
explanation: Group1, Group2, and Group3 only is correct because group-based licensing in Microsoft Entra ID supports security groups (including mail-enabled security groups) and Microsoft 365 groups that have securityEnabled=TRUE. • Group1 is a security group with security enabled, so it can be used. • Group2 is a mail-enabled security group, which is still a type of security group, and Microsoft documentation confirms that it is supported for license assignment. • Group3 is a Microsoft 365 group with security enabled, so it also qualifies. Group1 only is incorrect because Group3 (a security-enabled Microsoft 365 group) and Group2 (a mail-enabled security group) are also supported. Group1 and Group3 only is incorrect because Group2 is also eligible for license assignment, as mail- enabled security groups are supported. Group3 and Group4 only is incorrect because Group4 is a Microsoft 365 group with security disabled, making it ineligible. Group1, Group2, Group3, and Group4 is incorrect because Group4 is security-disabled and cannot be used for license assignment.

question:
You have an Azure Load Balancer named LB1.

A user named User1 has the following role assignments:

• Virtual Machine Contributor assigned at the resource group level that contains LB1 (this

assignment is inherited by LB1)

Based on these role assignments and their scopes, select the answer choice that completes the

options.D: create a NAT rule for LB1
options.E: assign access permissions to other users for LB1

explanation: assign access permissions to other users for LB1 is the correct answer here. User1 has been assigned the User Access Administrator role on the specific resource, LB1. The User Access Administrator role allows User1 to manage access for other users on that resource, including assigning roles and permissions. This role provides the capability to delegate access without providing permissions to modify the resource itself. delete LB1 is incorrect because User1 does not have the Owner or Contributor role, which are required to delete resources in Azure. The assigned roles of User Access Administrator and Virtual Machine Contributor (at the resource group level) do not provide delete permissions for the Load Balancer. create a NAT rule for LB1 is incorrect because configuring or modifying NAT rules on a load balancer requires the Network Contributor or Load Balancer Contributor role. The User Access Administrator role does not allow User1 to configure or modify network settings, and the Virtual Machine Contributor role (inherited at the resource group level) also does not include permissions for network configurations.

Based on these role assignments and their scopes, select the answer choice that completes the

options.D: Tenant Root Group, ManagementGroup1, Subscription1, and RG1 only
options.E: Tenant Root Group, ManagementGroup1, Subscription1, RG1, and VM1

explanation: Tenant Root Group, ManagementGroup1, Subscription1, RG1, and VM1 is correct because Azure Policy definitions can be assigned at any level in the Azure hierarchy, including the tenant root group, management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, and individual resource. It should be noted that policy cannot be applied to an individual resource from the Azure Portal, however, it can be done via Azure CLI or PowerShell. Which Azure resources can you specify as exclusions from Policy1?

options.D: ManagementGroup1, Subscription1, RG1, and VM1 only
options.E: Tenant Root Group, ManagementGroup1, Subscription1, RG1, and VM1

explanation: ManagementGroup1, Subscription1, RG1, and VM1 only is correct because when assigning a policy, you can exclude resources at any level in the hierarchy, including management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, and individual resources. Exclusions are designed to provide flexibility in policy enforcement by allowing specific resources or groups to be excluded from a policy's scope. Tenant Root Group cannot be excluded from policy assignments. Exclusions are applicable to management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, and individual resources only.

question:
Your Azure environment contains 20 Windows Server virtual machines, an existing network security

group called NSG1, and two virtual networks — VNET1 and VNET2 — that are connected through

peering.

You intend to deploy an Azure Bastion host using the Basic SKU into VNET1. To ensure the Bastion

service is reachable from external networks, you need to update NSG1 to allow incoming traffic from

the internet.

When creating the inbound rule in NSG1, which destination port must be allowed?
explanation: 443 is correct because Azure Bastion uses HTTPS on port 443 for secure communication from the user's browser to the Azure Bastion host. This allows secure RDP or SSH access to virtual machines in the virtual network without exposing these VMs directly to the internet. When deploying Azure Bastion, an inbound rule must be added to the NSG for port 443 to allow this secure connection from the internet to the Bastion host. 22 is incorrect because port 22 is used for SSH connections, but with Azure Bastion, the communication is tunneled over port 443 via HTTPS, making SSH directly over port 22 unnecessary. 3389 is incorrect because port 3389 is used for RDP connections. Azure Bastion tunnels RDP sessions over port 443, eliminating the need to open port 3389 in the NSG. 8080 is incorrect because port 8080 is not used by Azure Bastion for any connection.

• Storage Blob Data Reader

• Storage Table Data Contributor

• Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor

A shared access signature (SAS) named SAS1 is created for storage1 with the configuration shown in

the exhibit.

Which of the following resources can User1 write to by using SAS1?
explanation: Table1 only is correct because the SAS policy shown in the exhibit explicitly grants permissions only for the Table service. This means that when connecting to the storage account using SAS1, the scope of access is restricted to Table-based resources, such as Table1. Other services, such as Blob or File (which include container1 and folder1, respectively), are not included in the SAS policy. Therefore, only Table1 is accessible for all permitted operations, including creating, reading, updating, and deleting (CRUD). Other services will not be visible or accessible when connecting using this SAS key.

Which storage accounts meet this requirement?
explanation: storage1, storage2, and storage3 is correct because all three storage account types—StorageV2, BlobStorage, and BlockBlobStorage—support lifecycle management policies for block blobs and append blobs. question:

options.B: blob storage and file storage only
options.C: file storage and table storage only
options.D: blob storage, table storage, and queue storage only
options.E: blob storage, file storage, table storage, and queue storage

question:
An Azure Storage account stores approximately 10,000 blob objects and is accessed by several

different users.

You must implement a solution that restricts visibility so that each user can list and access only certain

blobs according to their assigned blob index tags.

What component or configuration should you implement to meet this requirement?
explanation: a role assignment condition is correct because role assignment conditions in Azure can enforce granular access control based on blob index tags. By using conditions in role assignments, you can ensure that users are restricted to viewing only the blobs that match specific index tags. This is an advanced Azure Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) feature designed for fine-grained access control scenarios. a stored access policy is incorrect because stored access policies are used in conjunction with Shared Access Signatures (SAS) to manage shared access over time, but they cannot enforce access based on blob index tags. just-in-time (JIT) virtual machine access is incorrect because JIT VM access is designed to provide temporary access to virtual machines and has no relevance to blob access control or index tags. a shared access signature (SAS) is incorrect because while SAS can provide temporary access to blobs, it cannot enforce blob index tag-based conditions for granular access control.

question:
In an Azure subscription named Subscription1, there is a resource group named RG1.

Inside RG1, two load balancers are deployed:

• LB1 – configured as an internal load balancer

• LB2 – configured as a public load balancer

You need to grant a user named Admin1 the ability to add and configure a backend address pool

for LB1 by using backend resources in RG1. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.

To enable Admin1 to create and configure a backend address pool for LB1, which Azure RBAC role

should be assigned?

options.A: Contributor role assigned at the LB1 scope
options.B: Network Contributor role assigned at the LB1 scope
options.C: Network Contributor role assigned at the RG1 scope
options.D: Owner role assigned at the LB1 scope

explanation: Network Contributor role assigned at the RG1 scope is correct because adding a backend pool to a load balancer requires permissions not only on the load balancer itself but also on the resources (e.g., virtual machines or virtual machine scale sets) that will be added to the backend pool. The Network Contributor role at the resource group (RG1) level ensures Admin1 has the necessary permissions to manage network resources across RG1, including both the load balancer and the backend pool resources, while still adhering to the principle of least privilege. Contributor role assigned at the LB1 scope is incorrect because this role grants overly broad permissions beyond just managing network resources. It does not align with the principle of least privilege. Owner role assigned at the LB1 scope is incorrect because the Owner role allows full control, including assigning roles, which exceeds the requirements for adding a backend pool. Network Contributor role assigned at the LB1 scope is incorrect because while this role provides permissions to manage the load balancer, it does not include permissions for managing the backend pool's underlying resources (e.g., virtual machines). These additional permissions are required to successfully add resources to the backend pool.

question:
In an Azure subscription named Subscription1, there is a resource group named RG1.

Inside RG1, two load balancers are deployed:

• LB1 – configured as an internal load balancer

• LB2 – configured as a public load balancer

You need to grant Admin1 the ability to create a health probe on LB2. The solution must follow the

principle of least privilege.

Which Azure RBAC role should assignment be assigned to Admin1 to allow the creation of a health

probe on LB2?

options.A: Contributor role assigned at the LB2 scope
options.B: Network Contributor role assigned at the LB2 scope
options.C: Network Contributor role assigned at the RG1 scope
options.D: Owner role assigned at the LB2 scope

explanation: Network Contributor role assigned at the LB2 scope is correct because it adheres to the principle of least privilege. This role provides sufficient permissions to configure and manage health probes on the specific load balancer without granting unnecessary access to the entire resource group or other unrelated network resources. The Network Contributor role at the resource group level ensures Admin1 has the necessary access to both the load balancer and the related network resources, adhering to the principle of least privilege. Network Contributor role assigned at the RG1 scope is incorrect because assigning this role at the resource group level grants broader permissions than necessary. While it enables the required operations, it goes against the principle of least privilege by providing access to all network resources within the resource group, not just LB2. Contributor role assigned at the LB2 scope is incorrect because it grants excessive permissions, including access to non-network-related tasks, violating the principle of least privilege. Owner role assigned at the LB2 scope is incorrect because the Owner role provides full administrative control, including the ability to assign roles, which far exceeds the permissions needed to add a health probe.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that includes 10 virtual machines running Windows Server. Each VM

hosts a website using IIS, and the Azure Monitor Agent is already installed on all machines.

Your objective is to collect IIS log files from each virtual machine and store them in a Log Analytics

workspace.

What should you configure as the initial step?

options.E: an Azure Monitor Private Link Scope (AMPLS)

explanation: Diagnostic settings is the correct answer because Diagnostic settings in Azure allow you to specify which logs and metrics should be collected from your virtual machines and where they should be sent, such as a Log Analytics workspace. To collect IIS logs from each virtual machine and store them in a Log Analytics workspace, you must configure Diagnostic settings on each virtual machine to enable and route IIS log data appropriately. a private endpoint is incorrect because private endpoints are used to provide private access to Azure services via a private IP address, which is unrelated to configuring IIS log collection. a data collection endpoint is incorrect because a Data Collection Endpoint (DCE) is only needed if Azure Monitor Private Links are in use, which is not specified in this scenario. VM insights is incorrect because VM insights focuses on performance monitoring and dependency mapping for virtual machines. It does not handle IIS log collection and routing to a Log Analytics workspace. an Azure Monitor Private Link Scope (AMPLS) is incorrect because AMPLS enables private access to Azure Monitor resources using Private Links. It is not a requirement for IIS log collection in this context.

chapter: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
question:
You plan to deploy multiple Azure virtual machines running Windows Server 2022 as part of a virtual

machine scale set by using an Azure Resource Manager template.

You must ensure that NGINX is installed and available on all virtual machines after the deployment

completes.

Which two options should you use?
explanation: a Desired State Configuration (DSC) extension is the correct answer because the DSC extension allows you to define a desired state configuration for virtual machines in a scale set. This configuration can include installing and configuring software like NGINX on all virtual machines automatically after deployment. the Publish-AzVMDscConfiguration cmdlet is also correct because this cmdlet is used to upload and publish a DSC configuration script to an Azure storage account. This script can then be used by the DSC extension to ensure NGINX is installed and configured on the virtual machines in the scale set. Azure Application Insights is incorrect because Application Insights is a monitoring service used to track application performance and detect issues. It does not install or configure software like NGINX on virtual machines. the New-AzConfigurationAssignment cmdlet is incorrect because this cmdlet is used to assign configurations in Azure Policy for governance, not for installing or configuring software on virtual machines.

chapter: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
question:
You have a subnet named Subnet1 that hosts several Azure virtual machines. A network security group

named NSG1 is associated with Subnet1, and NSG1 currently includes only the default security rules.

You must add a rule to NSG1 that blocks the virtual machines in Subnet1 from accessing the Azure

portal. At the same time, the virtual machines must continue to have access to other destinations on the

internet.

What value should you configure for the Destination setting in the rule?
explanation: Service Tag is the correct answer because Service Tags simplify network security group (NSG) rules by allowing you to reference a group of IP addresses associated with a specific Azure service. In this scenario, to block access to the Azure portal while still allowing access to other internet resources, you would use the AzureCloud service tag as the Destination in your NSG rule. This ensures that traffic specifically destined for the Azure portal is denied without impacting other internet traffic. Application security group is incorrect because Application Security Groups (ASGs) are used to group virtual machines within the same virtual network to simplify NSG management. They cannot be used to target Azure services like the Azure portal. IP Addresses is incorrect because blocking access to the Azure portal using IP addresses would require you to manually identify and maintain the list of Azure portal IP ranges, which is not practical or recommended. Any is incorrect because setting the destination to "Any" would block all internet traffic, including non- Azure-related services, which does not meet the requirement of allowing access to other internet hosts.

question:
You have two Azure virtual machines named VM1 and VM2, and two Recovery Services vaults

named RSV1 and RSV2.

Currently, VM2 is protected by backups stored in RSV1.

You want to configure backups for VM2 by using RSV2 instead.

What action should you perform first?

options.A: From the RSV1 blade, click Backup items and stop the VM2 backup.
options.B: From the RSV2 blade, click Backup. From the Backup blade, select the backup for the
options.C: virtual machine, and then click Backup.
options.D: From the VM2 blade, click Disaster recovery, click Replication settings, and then select
options.E: RSV2 as the Recovery Services vault.
options.F: From the RSV1 blade, click Backup Jobs and export the VM2 job.

explanation: From the RSV1 blade, click Backup items and stop the VM2 backup is the correct answer because an Azure virtual machine can only be backed up to one Recovery Services vault at a time. To back up VM2 to a different vault (RSV2), you must first stop the existing backup in RSV1. Once the backup is stopped and the backup data is removed, you can reconfigure the backup for VM2 in RSV2. From the RSV2 blade, click Backup. From the Backup blade, select the backup for the virtual machine, and then click Backup is incorrect because you cannot directly configure VM2 to back up in RSV2 without first stopping the existing backup configuration in RSV1. From the VM2 blade, click Disaster recovery, click Replication settings, and then select RSV2 as the Recovery Services vault is incorrect because Disaster Recovery settings are for replicating a VM to another region, not for configuring backup to a Recovery Services vault. From the RSV1 blade, click Backup Jobs and export the VM2 job is incorrect because exporting backup jobs does not change the Recovery Services vault assigned to the virtual machine.

question:
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 with the subscription ID 8f3a1c92-5d47-4b6e-

a2f9-71c3d8e5ab40.

You want to create a custom Azure RBAC role named CustomRole1 that meets the following

conditions:

• The role can be assigned only at the resource group scope within Sub1.

• The role must not allow users to manage access permissions (RBAC) on the resource groups.

• The role must allow users to view, create, update, and delete resources inside the resource groups.

You are defining the role by using a JSON definition that includes

the assignableScopes and permissions sections.

What value should you specify for Code Segment A in the definition of CustomRole1?

"/"
explanation: "/subscriptions/8f3a1c92-5d47-4b6e-a2f9-71c3d8e5ab40" is the correct answer here. The assignableScopes property defines where a custom role can be assigned, and it accepts scopes such as management groups, subscriptions, or specific resource groups. Since Subscription1 has a subscription ID of 8f3a1c92-5d47-4b6e-a2f9-71c3d8e5ab40, and the requirement is to allow assignment of the role only to resource groups within this subscription, the correct assignable scope is the subscription level. This ensures the custom role is available for assignment at the resource group level within that subscription without being overly permissive. "/" is incorrect because the root scope is not supported in custom role definitions. AssignableScopes cannot be set to "/", and attempting to do so will result in a validation error. "/subscriptions/8f3a1c92-5d47-4b6e-a2f9-71c3d8e5ab40/resourceGroups" is incorrect because this is not a valid scope. The string "resourceGroups" is a collection placeholder, and not a valid scope by itself. Using it will result in a validation error such as: "Validation error: Invalid scope: /subscriptions/<SubscriptionID>/resourceGroups". Additionally, the question does not reference any specific resource group. It refers broadly to "resource groups" within the subscription, and therefore the assignable scope must be set at the subscription level.

question:
You have an Azure subscription named Sub1 with the subscription ID 8f3a1c92-5d47-4b6e-

a2f9-71c3d8e5ab40.

You want to create a custom Azure RBAC role named CustomRole1 that meets the following

conditions:

• The role can be assigned only at the resource group scope within Sub1.

• The role must not allow users to manage access permissions (RBAC) on the resource groups.

• The role must allow users to view, create, update, and delete resources inside the resource groups.

You are defining the role by using a JSON definition that includes

the assignableScopes and permissions sections.

What value should you specify for Code Segment B in the definition of CustomRole1?
explanation: "Microsoft.Authorization/" is the correct answer here. In the context of custom RBAC role definitions, the "notActions" element (Dropdown 2) is used to explicitly deny certain management operations, even if the "actions" list includes a wildcard like "*". In this scenario, the custom role CustomRole1 must allow full access to view, create, modify, and delete resources within resource groups, but it must prevent the user from managing access permissions (i.e., prevent role assignments). Role assignment and access control operations in Azure are managed through the Microsoft.Authorization namespace. Therefore, to block permission management, you need to specify "Microsoft.Authorization/" in the "notActions" array. This removes the ability to read, create, or delete role assignments, while still allowing other actions. "Microsoft.Resources/" is incorrect because this namespace is used for general resource management tasks like creating and managing resource groups or deployments, not for managing access control. Including it in "notActions" would block legitimate resource operations that the role should be allowed to perform. "Microsoft.Security/*" is incorrect because it relates to security center operations such as policy management, security recommendations, and alerts. It is not relevant to access control and does not affect permissions related to RBAC.

chapter: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
question:
You have an Azure web app named App1 that uses deployment slots, as shown below:

• webapp1-prod -> Production

• webapp1-test -> Staging

You validate multiple updates to App1 in the webapp1-test slot.

After completing testing, you create a backup of App1.

You then swap the webapp1-test slot with webapp1-prod, after which the application starts showing

performance problems.

You must roll back App1 to the earlier, stable version in the shortest possible time.

What action should you take?
explanation: Swap the deployment slots again is the correct answer here. Azure App Service deployment slots allow you to deploy and test changes in a staging slot (in this case, webapp1-test) and then swap the staging slot with the production slot (webapp1-prod) when ready. When a swap is performed, the content and configuration of the slots are exchanged, allowing for a quick rollback if needed. Since you already swapped the test slot into production and discovered performance issues, the fastest way to revert is to swap the slots again. This will return the original production version (which is now in the test slot) back to its place, restoring the last working state almost instantly and with zero downtime. Restore App1 from the backup is incorrect because although it can restore the app to a previous state, it is a slower operation and involves data loss risk and manual effort, making it less ideal for quick recovery. Create a clone of App1 is incorrect because cloning creates a new app instance, which is not a recovery mechanism and would not affect the current deployment state of App1. Redeploy the application to App1 is incorrect because this would require rebuilding and redeploying the application code, which takes more time and may not exactly match the last known good state.

question:
You have a pay-as-you-go Azure subscription with the following virtual machines:

• VM1 in resource group RG1, costing 20 euros per day

• VM2 in resource group RG2, costing 30 euros per day

You create the budget shown in the following exhibit.

The budget is set up with alert thresholds at 50%, 70%, and 100%, each linked to different action

groups.

The action group AG1 contains only the user admin@apexcore.com.

Based on this configuration, complete the following statement:

"When VM1 and VM2 reach the maximum budget limit, ___________________________________."

options.A: Both VM1 and VM2 are automatically shut down.
options.C: VM1 is stopped, while VM2 continues to run.

explanation: VM1 and VM2 continue running is the correct answer here. Azure budgets are a monitoring and alerting tool only. They do not enforce or take automatic action such as shutting down resources. In the case study: • Budget1 is scoped to Resource Group RG1, which contains VM1. • VM2, which is in RG2, is not within the scope of the budget and is therefore not tracked or managed by this budget. • Even when the budget is fully consumed (100%), the configured action groups (AG1, AG2, AG3) only send notifications (via Email, SMS, or Azure app), but do not stop or deallocate any virtual machines. Therefore, when both VM1 and VM2 reach their maximum cost, they continue to run, and no automatic shutdown occurs.

question:
You have a pay-as-you-go Azure subscription with the following virtual machines:

• VM1 in resource group RG1, costing 20 euros per day

• VM2 in resource group RG2, costing 30 euros per day

You create the budget shown in the following exhibit.

The budget is set up with alert thresholds at 50%, 70%, and 100%, each linked to different action

groups.

The action group AG1 contains only the user admin@apexcore.com.

Based on this configuration, complete the following statement:

"Given the existing usage costs of the virtual machines, _________________________."

options.A: no email notifications will be sent each month
options.B: one email notification will be sent each month
options.C: two email notifications will be sent each month
options.D: three email notifications will be sent each month

explanation: one email notification will be sent each month is the correct answer here. This is a common area of confusion, so let's clarify it step by step to avoid misinterpretation. In the provided scenario: • VM1 is the only virtual machine within the scope of Budget1 (since VM1 is in RG1, and the budget is scoped to RG1). • VM1 costs €20 per day, which totals approximately €600 per month. • The budget thresholds are: ◦ 50% of €1,000 → triggers Action Group AG1 (configured to send 1 email) ◦ 70% of €1,000 → triggers AG2 (sends 1 SMS) ◦ 100% of €1,000 → triggers AG3 (sends 1 Azure app notification) At €600, only the 50% threshold is crossed, which triggers AG1. Why it's not two emails: You may mistakenly think that: 1. One email is sent because AG1 is triggered 2. Another email is sent because admin@apexcore.com is listed as an alert recipient This is not correct. In Azure Budgets, email alerts are sent only via Action Groups. The person listed (e.g., admin@apexcore.com) in the budget configuration is part of the Action Group (AG1) that is associated with the 50% threshold. They are not receiving a second, separate notification outside the Action Group. So even though the name appears in the recipient list, it does not represent an additional notification beyond what AG1 is configured to send.

chapter: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
question:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the following App Service plans:

• ASP1 runs on Linux and uses the Basic B1 pricing tier.

• ASP2 runs on Windows and uses the Standard S1 pricing tier.

• ASP3 runs on Linux and uses the Premium v3 pricing tier.

You plan to create an additional App Service plan with these settings:

• Name: ASP4

• Operating system: Windows

• Pricing tier: Premium v3

You need to determine which of the App Service plans support rule-based scale-out.

Which App Service plans should you identify?
explanation: ASP2, ASP3, and ASP4 only is correct. The question asks which App Service plans support rule- based scale out, which refers specifically to autoscale—the ability to automatically increase or decrease the number of instances based on predefined rules, such as CPU usage, memory load, or a schedule. According to Microsoft documentation: • Autoscale is not supported in the Basic (B1) pricing tier. While Basic plans support manual scale-out (up to 3 instances), they do not support rule-based scaling. • Standard (S1) and Premium v3 plans do support autoscale, allowing automatic instance management based on defined rules and schedules. Therefore, ASP2, ASP3, and ASP4 all support rule-based scale out, while ASP1 does not.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the following App Service plans:

• ASP1 runs on Linux and uses the Basic B1 pricing tier.

• ASP2 runs on Windows and uses the Standard S1 pricing tier.

• ASP3 runs on Linux and uses the Premium v3 pricing tier.

You plan to create an additional App Service plan with these settings:

• Name: ASP4

• Operating system: Windows

• Pricing tier: Premium v3

You need to determine which of the App Service plans support zone redundancy.

Which App Service plans should you identify?
explanation: ASP4 only is the correct answer here. Azure App Service supports zone redundancy only on the Premium v2 and Premium v3 pricing tiers. This makes ASP3 and ASP4 eligible, since both are using the Premium v3 tier. But since the correct combination (ASP3 and ASP4 only) is not available among the answer choices, we need to select the best possible correct option from the list. Among the choices provided: • ASP4 only is the most accurate, because while it omits ASP3, it is the only option that exclusively lists a supported plan. Therefore, ASP4 only is the best and most appropriate answer based on the available options.

question:
You have an Azure subscription with a virtual network named VNet1.

VNet1 includes four subnets named Gateway, Perimeter, NVA, and Production.

The NVA subnet hosts two network virtual appliances (NVAs).

These NVAs are used to inspect network traffic flowing between the Perimeter subnet and

the Production subnet.

You need to deploy an Azure Load Balancer in front of the NVAs.

The solution must meet the following conditions:

• The NVAs must operate in an active-active setup with automatic failover.

• Traffic must be load balanced to two different services in the Production subnet, and each

service uses a different IP address.

Which three actions should you take?

options.A: Add a frontend IP configuration, two backend pools, and a health probe
options.B: Add a frontend IP configuration, a backend pool, and a health probe
options.E: Add two load balancing rules that have HA Ports enabled and Floating IP disabled
options.F: Add two load balancing rules that have HA Ports and Floating IP enabled

explanation: Add a frontend IP configuration, two backend pools, and a health probe is correct because the requirement involves load balancing traffic to two services on different IP addresses in the Production subnet. This necessitates two separate backend pools, each associated with one of the services. A frontend IP configuration is needed to receive incoming traffic, and a health probe is essential to determine the availability of the NVAs in the backend pool for failover. Deploy a standard load balancer is correct because only the Standard SKU load balancer supports advanced features like HA Ports, Floating IP, and availability zones, all of which are needed for this high availability active-active NVA setup. The Basic SKU does not support multiple backend pools or advanced configurations required in this scenario. Add two load balancing rules that have HA Ports and Floating IP enabled is correct because: • HA Ports allows the load balancer to listen on all ports for the services, ensuring full connectivity through the NVAs. • Floating IP (also known as Direct Server Return) must be enabled for scenarios that involve high availability and active-active NVAs, because it ensures the return path of packets doesn't interfere with source NAT. Add a frontend IP configuration, a backend pool, and a health probe is incorrect because a single backend pool cannot load balance traffic to two distinct IP addresses (services). This setup lacks the isolation needed for managing traffic across both services. Deploy a basic load balancer is incorrect because Basic SKU does not support HA Ports or multiple backend pools, which are essential for this solution. Add two load balancing rules that have HA Ports enabled and Floating IP disabled is incorrect because disabling Floating IP prevents the correct routing behavior necessary for high availability and direct server return, which is needed in an active-active NVA configuration.

question:
You have the following Azure virtual networks configured:

• VNet1

◦ Address space: 10.11.0.0/16

◦ Subnet: 10.11.0.0/17

◦ Resource group Azure region: West US

• VNet2

◦ Address space: 10.11.0.0/17

◦ Subnet: 10.11.0.0/25

◦ Resource group Azure region: West US

• VNet3

◦ Address space: 10.10.0.0/22

◦ Subnet: 10.10.1.0/24

◦ Resource group Azure region: East US

• VNet4

◦ Address space: 192.168.16.0/22

◦ Subnet: 192.168.16.0/24

◦ Resource group Azure region: North Europe

You want to configure virtual network peering for VNet1.

Which of the listed virtual networks can be peered with VNet1?
explanation: VNet3 and VNet4 only is the correct answer here. To peer virtual networks in Azure, one of the main requirements is that the address spaces must not overlap. In the case of VNet1 (10.11.0.0/16): • VNet2 (10.11.0.0/17) has an address space that overlaps with VNet1. Peering is not allowed in this case due to the overlapping IP ranges, even though it's in the same region. • VNet3 (10.10.0.0/22) has a non-overlapping address space and is in a different region (East US), which is still supported via global virtual network peering. • VNet4 (192.168.16.0/22) also has a non-overlapping address space and is in North Europe, which again supports global VNet peering. Therefore, only VNet3 and VNet4 can be peered with VNet1.

chapter: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
question:
You have two Azure subscriptions named Sub1 and Sub2.

In Sub1, there is a virtual machine named VM1 and a storage account named storage1.

The virtual machine VM1 is associated with the following resources:

• Disk1, which is the operating system disk for VM1

• NetInt1, which is the network interface attached to VM1

• VNet1, which is the virtual network that VM1 connects to

You need to move VM1 from Sub1 to Sub2.

Which of the associated resources must you move to Sub2 to complete this task?
explanation: VM1, Disk1, NetInt1, and VNet1 is the correct answer here. When you move a virtual machine (VM1) to another subscription, all its associated dependent resources must be moved as well. This includes the OS disk (Disk1), the network interface (NetInt1), and the virtual network (VNet1). Azure requires that all dependent resources are part of the move operation to ensure the VM remains functional in the target subscription. If any dependency, like the NIC or virtual network, is left behind, the VM will lose connectivity or fail validation during the move.

question:
You manage two Azure subscriptions: Subscription1 and Subscription2.

In Subscription1, the following resource groups exist:

• RG1 – Region: West Europe – Lock: None

• RG2 – Region: West Europe – Lock: Read-only

The resource group RG1 contains a web application named App1, which is deployed in the West

Europe region.

In Subscription2, the following resource groups are configured:

• RG3 – Region: North Europe – Lock: Delete

• RG4 – Region: Central US – Lock: None

True or False:

"App1 can be moved to RG2."
explanation: False is the correct answer because RG2 has a Read Only lock applied. When a resource group is locked with Read Only, you cannot add or move any resources into it. This type of lock prevents all write operations, including the action of moving a resource (such as App1) into the locked resource group. Even though App1 and RG2 are in the same region and subscription, the lock on RG2 blocks the move.

question:
You manage two Azure subscriptions: Subscription1 and Subscription2.

In Subscription1, the following resource groups exist:

• RG1 – Region: West Europe – Lock: None

• RG2 – Region: West Europe – Lock: Read-only

The resource group RG1 contains a web application named App1, which is deployed in the West

Europe region.

In Subscription2, the following resource groups are configured:

• RG3 – Region: North Europe – Lock: Delete

• RG4 – Region: Central US – Lock: None

True or False:

"App1 can be moved to RG3."
explanation: True is the correct answer because Azure allows moving supported resources, such as an App Service web app, between resource groups and even between subscriptions within the same tenant. When a resource is moved between resource groups or subscriptions, the resource itself does not move to another region. Only the Azure Resource Manager metadata changes, and the resource continues to run in its original region. In this scenario, App1 is deployed in the West Europe region, and moving it to RG3 does not change its location. Even though RG3 is associated with North Europe, resource groups can contain resources from different regions, so this does not prevent the move. Additionally, if the web app depends on other resources, such as an App Service Plan, those dependent resources must be moved together in the same operation. The Delete lock on RG3 does not block the move because a delete lock only prevents deletion of the resource group or its resources. It does not prevent adding or moving resources into the resource group. Therefore, App1 can be moved to RG3, making the statement True.

question:
You manage two Azure subscriptions: Subscription1 and Subscription2.

In Subscription1, the following resource groups exist:

• RG1 – Region: West Europe – Lock: None

• RG2 – Region: West Europe – Lock: Read-only

The resource group RG1 contains a web application named App1, which is deployed in the West

Europe region.

In Subscription2, the following resource groups are configured:

• RG3 – Region: North Europe – Lock: Delete

• RG4 – Region: Central US – Lock: None

True or False:

"App1 can be moved to RG4."
explanation: True is the correct answer because App1 can be moved to RG4, which is located in the Central US region, provided that RG4 does not contain any existing App Service resources such as web apps, App Service plans, or TLS/SSL certificates. Although App1 is in West Europe, moving an app across resource groups or subscriptions does not change the region of the app. The app retains its original region (West Europe) after the move. The metadata such as resource group or subscription may change, but the physical location of the app stays the same. There is no lock on RG4, so it won't block the operation.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that contains a virtual machine named VM1.

The virtual machine has two disks attached:

• An operating system disk named Disk1

• A data disk named Disk2

You are required to back up only Disk2 by using Azure Backup.

Which three actions should you perform in sequence?
explanation: 3-1-4 is the correct sequence of actions. (Action 3) Create an Azure Backup vault is correct. For Azure Disk Backup (as opposed to full VM backup), you use an Azure Backup vault, which is a specific vault type designed for backing up individual managed disks. This is different from a Recovery Services vault, which is used for broader scenarios like VM, SQL, and file backups. (Action 1) Create a backup policy and configure the backup is correct. After the vault is created, you define a backup policy that dictates the schedule and retention for the disk backup. You then associate Disk2 with this policy. (Action 4) Configure a managed identity is correct. Azure Disk Backup uses Azure RBAC and managed identities for access. You must configure a user-assigned managed identity with appropriate roles (like Disk Backup Reader) to allow the vault to access and back up Disk2. (Action 2) Create a Recovery Services vault is incorrect. This is used for VM-level backup and is not applicable to Azure Disk Backup, which requires a Backup vault. (Action 5) Delegate permissions for the vault is incorrect. Disk Backup uses managed identity and RBAC instead of manual permission delegation. You assign roles to the managed identity instead of explicitly delegating permissions.

question:
You have deployed Azure virtual machines across three different Azure regions.

In each region:

• There is one virtual network.

• Each virtual network contains multiple subnets.

• All virtual networks are connected using full-mesh VNet peering.

A user reports that they are unable to connect over TCP port 33000 from a virtual machine in one

region to a virtual machine in another region.

Which two options can you use to investigate and troubleshoot this connectivity issue?
explanation: IP flow verify is correct because it allows you to test whether traffic is allowed to or from a virtual machine based on NSG (Network Security Group) rules. It specifically helps in identifying whether a particular port (like 33000) is blocked or allowed, which is essential for troubleshooting connectivity between VMs. Connection troubleshoot is correct because it helps diagnose issues with connectivity between two endpoints. It checks DNS resolution, network latency, and whether TCP connections (like on port 33000) can be established, making it ideal for this scenario involving cross-region VM communication. Azure Monitor Network Insights is incorrect because it gives you a high-level view of the health and topology of your network resources, but it doesn't perform port-level diagnostics or simulate connection attempts. effective security rules is incorrect because it shows the final set of NSG rules applied to a NIC or subnet but doesn't actively test whether a specific port is blocked or allowed. It's useful for analysis, but not direct diagnostics. Azure Virtual Network Manager is incorrect because it's used for centralized network management and policy enforcement across VNets, not for diagnosing connectivity issues like blocked ports.

question:
You have an Azure subscription called Subscription1 that includes two virtual machines named VM1

and VM2, both running Windows Server 2016.

VM1 is protected with Azure Backup, configured to run daily backups without using the Azure Backup

agent.

VM1 has been compromised by ransomware that encrypts data.

You need to restore data from the most recent backup of VM1.

To which of the following targets can you perform a file-level recovery for VM1?

options.B: VM1 or a new Azure virtual machine only
options.D: A new Azure virtual machine only
options.E: Any Windows computer that has Internet connectivity

explanation: Any Windows computer that has Internet connectivity is the correct answer because Azure Backup supports file-level recovery from a VM backup even when the Azure Backup agent is not used. The recovery is performed by downloading and running a script provided by the portal, which mounts the backup snapshot as a virtual drive. This can be done on any supported Windows machine with internet access, allowing files to be copied to any desired location.

question:
You have an Azure subscription called Subscription1 that includes two virtual machines named VM1

and VM2, both running Windows Server 2016.

VM1 is protected with Azure Backup, configured to run daily backups without using the Azure Backup

agent.

VM1 has been compromised by ransomware that encrypts data.

You need to restore data from the most recent backup of VM1.

To which location can you restore the backup?

options.B: VM1 or a new Azure virtual machine only
options.D: Any Windows computer that has Internet connectivity

explanation: VM1 or a new Azure virtual machine only is the correct answer because when Azure Backup is used to back up a VM without using the Azure Backup agent, it performs a full image-level backup of the virtual machine. In the event of data loss (e.g., ransomware), the entire VM can be restored either to the original VM (VM1) or as a new Azure virtual machine from the latest recovery point. This method does not support file-level recovery to arbitrary machines unless the MARS agent is used, which is not applicable in this scenario. VM1 only is incorrect because Azure Backup allows restoring the VM to a new VM as well, not just to the original one. VM1 and VM2 only is incorrect because Azure Backup does not allow restoring a VM backup to a different existing VM like VM2. Restores are limited to the original VM or a new one. Any Windows computer that has Internet connectivity is incorrect because that type of file-level restore is only supported when using the Azure Backup agent (MARS) or the System Center DPM/ MABS, which is not being used in this scenario.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that contains the following resources:

You configure Azure Site Recovery to replicate VM1 from East US to West US.

You then initiate a test failover and choose VNET2 as the destination virtual network.

After the test failover completes, to which subnet in VNET2 will the test instance of VM1 be connected?
explanation: DemoSubnet1 is the correct answer because when performing a test failover in Azure Site Recovery and no matching subnet name exists in the target virtual network (VNET2), the test virtual machine is automatically connected to the first subnet in alphabetical order. In this case, the source subnet is Subnet2, which does not exist in VNET2. Among the available subnets in VNET2—DemoSubnet1, RecoverySubnetA, RecoverySubnetB, and TestSubnet1—the one that comes first alphabetically is DemoSubnet1, so the test VM is connected there. RecoverySubnetA is incorrect because although it contains "Recovery" in the name, it comes after DemoSubnet1 alphabetically. RecoverySubnetB is incorrect because it is not the first subnet in alphabetical order and does not match the source subnet name. TestSubnet1 is incorrect because ASR does not prioritize subnets based on naming conventions like "Test". It only looks for an exact match or falls back to the first subnet in alphabetical order.

package assignment:

The external user lifecycle settings are configured so that when an external user loses their last access

package assignment:

• The user is removed from the directory after 30 days.

True or False:

"After the 365-day assignment period ends, users from ironclad.com will be removed from Group1."
explanation: False is the correct answer. When you assign ironclad users to Group1 through an access package, their assignment is set to expire after 365 days. At that point, the users' access package assignment expires, which means: • They lose access to Group1 and other resources tied to the package. • Their membership in Group1 is revoked immediately at expiration. However, this is not the same as being "removed" from the tenant. The external user lifecycle settings add another step: • After the assignment expires, external users remain in the tenant directory for an additional 30 days. • During that time, they cannot access Group1 because their assignment has expired, but their guest account still exists in the directory. • Only after day 395 (365 + 30) are they actually removed from the directory, which finalizes their removal from all groups.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that includes a resource group named ResGrp1.

ResGrp1 is located in the West Europe region and is used to host temporary resources for a project.

The resource group contains the following resources:

• VM1 is a virtual machine deployed in the North Europe region.

• RGV1 is a Recovery Services vault located in North Europe.

• SQLDB01 is a SQL Server running on an Azure virtual machine in North Europe.

• sa001 is a storage account deployed in West Europe.

The virtual machine SQLDB01 is configured to be backed up to the Recovery Services vault RGV1.

After the project is completed, you attempt to delete ResGrp1 from the Azure portal, but the deletion

operation fails.

You need to successfully remove ResGrp1.

What should you do first?
explanation: Stop the backup of SQLDB01 is correct because the deletion of a resource group that contains a Recovery Services vault with active backup jobs or protected items will fail. In this scenario, SQLDB01 is backed up to RGV1, which means there are active backup items associated with it. To successfully delete ResGrp1, you first need to stop the backup for SQLDB01 and delete any protected items from the Recovery Services vault (RGV1). Once the backup is stopped and protected items are removed, ResGrp1 can be deleted. Delete the VM1 virtual machine is incorrect because deleting VM1 would not impact the active backup configuration associated with SQLDB01 in RGV1. The deletion of the resource group fails due to the active backup in the Recovery Services vault, not because of the presence of VM1. Delete the sa001 storage account is incorrect because deleting the storage account in a different region (West Europe) does not address the active backup in RGV1. The storage account (sa001) is unrelated to the backup process of SQLDB01 and does not prevent the deletion of the resource group. Stop the VM1 virtual machine is incorrect because stopping the virtual machine does not affect the backup status in the Recovery Services vault. The issue lies with the active backup of SQLDB01, not with the state of VM1.

You have an Azure subscription that includes two storage accounts

named contoso101 and contoso102.

The subscription also contains two virtual machines with the following configurations:

• VM1 is connected to VNet1/Subnet1 and uses a Basic public IP address SKU.

• VM2 is connected to VNet1/Subnet2 and uses a Standard public IP address SKU.

Within VNet1, service endpoints are configured as follows:

• Microsoft.AzureActiveDirectory is enabled on Subnet2.

• Microsoft.Storage is enabled on Subnet1.

A service endpoint policy named Policy1 is created for the Microsoft.Storage service. The policy

allows access only to the storage account contoso101. The policy is associated with subnets that have

Microsoft.Storage service endpoints enabled.

True or False:

"VM1 can access contoso102."
explanation: False is the correct answer here. According to the information provided, the service endpoint policy is configured to allow access only to the contoso101 storage account through the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint associated with Subnet1 in VNet1. Since VM1 is connected to Subnet1 and the policy only permits access to contoso101, VM1 cannot access contoso102 because it is not included in the endpoint policy.

question:
You have an Azure subscription that includes two storage accounts

named contoso101 and contoso102.

The subscription also contains two virtual machines with the following configurations:

• VM1 is connected to VNet1/Subnet1 and uses a Basic public IP address SKU.

• VM2 is connected to VNet1/Subnet2 and uses a Standard public IP address SKU.

Within VNet1, service endpoints are configured as follows:

• Microsoft.AzureActiveDirectory is enabled on Subnet2.

• Microsoft.Storage is enabled on Subnet1.

A service endpoint policy named Policy1 is created for the Microsoft.Storage service. The policy

allows access only to the storage account contoso101. The policy is associated with subnets that have

Microsoft.Storage service endpoints enabled.

True or False:

"VM2 can access contoso101."
explanation: True is the correct answer. Service endpoint policies are always scoped to the subnet where they are applied, meaning they only control traffic originating from that specific subnet. In this scenario, the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint and its associated policy are applied to Subnet1, which contains VM1. Subnet2, where VM2 resides, has only an Azure Active Directory service endpoint and no storage endpoint or policy applied. This means the policy on Subnet1 does not restrict VM2's traffic. By default, subnets in the same virtual network can communicate freely unless explicit network security groups or custom routes block that communication, and no such restrictions are mentioned here. Because the question also does not state that the storage account firewall is locked down to specific networks, we assume the default configuration of allowing traffic from all networks. Under these conditions, VM2 can still reach contoso101 using the storage account's public endpoint, bypassing the need for a storage service endpoint or policy. The idea that Subnet1's policy would block all other subnets even via public endpoints, is a common misconception; Microsoft's documentation makes clear that service endpoint policies only affect traffic from the subnets to which they are applied. Therefore, the correct choice is that VM2 can indeed access contoso101.

• A virtual network named VNET1, which includes two subnets.

◦ subnet1 uses the IP address range 10.3.0.0/24.

◦ subnet2 uses the IP address range 10.4.0.0/24.

• A network security group named NSG1.

• A virtual machine named vm1 that has the private IP address 10.3.0.15 and is deployed in subnet1.

• A storage account named storage1.

The network security group NSG1 is configured with custom security rules as follows:

True or False:

"VM1 can access storage1."
explanation: True is the correct answer here. NSG1 has an outbound security rule named Storage_Access configured to allow TCP traffic on port 443 from the virtual network to resources tagged as Storage. This rule enables VM1 to access storage1 on port 443. Additionally, there is no inbound restriction on the Storage endpoint, so VM1 can successfully connect to storage1 as required.

You have an Azure subscription that contains the virtual machines shown in the following table.

You deploy a load balancer with the following characteristics:

• The load balancer is named LB1.

• It is an internal load balancer.

• It uses the Standard SKU.

• It is deployed in VNET1.

You need to ensure that both VM1 and VM2 can be added to the backend pool of LB1.

Proposed solution: You create a Basic SKU public IP address, associate it with the network interface

of VM1, and then start VM1.

Does this solution meet the requirement?
explanation: No is the correct answer here. For a Standard SKU load balancer, all virtual machines in the backend pool must be within the same region and connected to the same virtual network (VNET) as the load balancer itself. Additionally, they must either have a Standard SKU public IP address or no public IP address at all. In this scenario, associating a Basic SKU public IP address to VM1 does not meet the requirements for the Standard SKU load balancer. Therefore, this configuration does not allow VM1 and VM2 to be added to the backend pool of LB1.

You have an Azure subscription that contains 10 virtual networks, each deployed in its own resource

group.

Another administrator intends to create multiple network security groups (NSGs) within the subscription.

You must ensure that every newly created NSG automatically blocks TCP traffic on port 8080 between

the virtual networks.

Proposed solution: Assign a built-in Azure Policy definition at the subscription scope.

Does this solution satisfy the requirement?
explanation: No is the correct answer here. To meet the specific requirement of automatically blocking TCP port 8080 between virtual networks when an NSG is created, you would need to create a custom Azure policy. Built-in policies provided by Microsoft focus on general compliance and best practices and do not cover specific, custom configurations such as blocking a specific port across all new NSGs. Creating a custom policy allows you to define specific actions, such as blocking or allowing certain ports, tailored to your Azure environment's unique needs.

question:
You have an Azure subscription with the following resources in the same resource group (RG1):

• Vault1: A Recovery Services vault located in the East US region

• VM1: A virtual machine running Windows Server in the East US region

• VM2: A virtual machine running Windows Server in the West US region

On VM1, you configure Azure Backup to protect a folder named Folder1 using a scheduled file-and-

folder backup policy. The backup schedule is configured as follows:

• Backup frequency: Daily

• Backup times: 6:00 AM and 10:00 PM

You plan to restore this backup to a different virtual machine and want the data to be recovered

on VM2.

What is the first action you must take?

options.A: On VM2, install the Windows Server Backup feature.
options.B: On VM1, install the Microsoft Azure Recovery Services Agent.
options.C: On VM1, install the Windows Server Backup feature.
options.D: On VM2, install the Microsoft Azure Recovery Services Agent.

explanation: On VM2, install the Microsoft Azure Recovery Services Agent is correct because in order to restore a backup from the Recovery Services vault to a different virtual machine (in this case, VM2), you need to have the Microsoft Azure Recovery Services (MARS) Agent installed on the destination VM. This agent enables the VM to communicate with the Recovery Services vault, allowing it to access and restore backups stored in Azure. On VM2, install the Windows Server Backup feature is incorrect because the Windows Server Backup feature alone does not provide the necessary integration with Azure Recovery Services. The MARS Agent is required to retrieve backups from Azure. On VM1, install the Microsoft Azure Recovery Services Agent is incorrect as the MARS Agent is already installed on VM1 to perform the initial backup. The task here is to restore the backup to VM2. On VM1, install the Windows Server Backup feature is incorrect because this feature does not assist in restoring a backup to another VM. The backup is already configured on VM1, and the requirement is to restore it to VM2, which requires the MARS Agent on VM2.

question:
You have an Azure subscription named Subscription1 that is shared across multiple departments. The

subscription currently includes the following resources:

• storage1 - Azure Storage account

• RG1 - Resource group

• container1 - Blob container

• share1 - Azure file share

Another administrator deploys two new resources, a virtual machine named VM1 and a storage

account named storage2, by using a single Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template.

You want to review the ARM template that was used for this deployment.

From which Azure portal blade can you view the template associated with the deployment?
explanation: RG1 is correct because to view the Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template used for a deployment, you need to access the Resource Group (in this case, RG1) where the deployment was made. The Resource Group blade in the Azure portal includes an option to view the deployment history and allows you to access the templates used in those deployments. container1 is incorrect because a Blob container does not have deployment information or templates associated with it directly. It is a storage object within a storage account and lacks deployment-level insights. storage1 is incorrect as it is the storage account itself, and the ARM template used for deployments would not be accessible from the storage account blade. Templates are accessible through the Resource Group level. VM1 is incorrect because while you can see configuration and settings specific to VM1, the VM blade does not provide access to the ARM template used in the original deployment. The Resource Group blade is needed for viewing deployment templates.

question:
You have a public load balancer that distributes traffic on ports 80 and 443 across three virtual

machines named VM1, VM2, and VM3.

You want all Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) connections to be routed exclusively to VM3.

What configuration should you apply?

options.A: Create a separate public load balancer dedicated to VM3
options.B: Configure an additional frontend IP configuration

explanation: Configure an inbound NAT rule is correct because an inbound NAT rule allows you to direct specific traffic, such as RDP, to a particular virtual machine (VM3 in this case) behind the load balancer. By setting up an inbound NAT rule for port 3389 (RDP), you ensure that all RDP connections go directly to VM3 instead of balancing across all VMs. Create a separate public load balancer dedicated to VM3 is incorrect because creating a separate load balancer is unnecessary for directing RDP connections to VM3. An inbound NAT rule is sufficient to achieve this without additional load balancers. Configure an additional frontend IP configuration is incorrect as a frontend IP configuration is used to define the IP address on which the load balancer is accessible. It does not control how RDP traffic is directed to specific VMs. Configure a load balancing rule is incorrect because load balancing rules are intended for distributing traffic across multiple VMs based on specific ports, which is not the goal here. The objective is to direct all RDP traffic to VM3 specifically, not balance it across VMs.

question:

and resource groups.

The virtual networks are configured as follows:

• VNET1 is deployed in the West US region and belongs to resource group RG1.

• VNET2 is deployed in the Central US region and belongs to resource group RG1.

• VNET4 is deployed in the West US region and belongs to resource group RG2.

You plan to deploy an Azure Firewall named AF1 in resource group RG1, located in the West

US region.

Which virtual networks are valid targets for deploying AF1?
explanation: VNET1 only is correct because Azure Firewall can connect to a virtual network within the same region and resource group. In this scenario, AF1 is deployed in RG1 in the West US region. While VNET4 is also in the West US region, it is in a different resource group (RG2), which prevents AF1 from connecting to it. Therefore, VNET1 is the only virtual network eligible for connection to AF1.

explanation: From the Directory role blade, modify the directory role is correct because to assign an administrative role, such as the User Administrator role, to AdminUsr1, you need to navigate to the Directory role blade in the user account properties. options.D: MG1, Sub1, RG1, and VM1 only

explanation: Sub1, RG1, and VM1 only is correct because locks can be applied at the subscription, resource group, and resource (such as a virtual machine) levels to prevent accidental deletion or modification. In this case, Sub1 (the subscription), RG1 (the resource group), and VM1 (the virtual machine) are valid targets for applying locks to track usage and prevent deletion. RG1 and VM1 only is incorrect because locks can also be applied at the subscription level (Sub1), not just at the resource group and resource levels. Tenant Root Group, MG1, Sub1, RG1, and VM1 is incorrect because locks cannot be applied to the Tenant Root Group or management groups.

machines to the backend pool of LB1.

You have an Azure subscription named Subscription1 that contains a virtual machine named VM1.

On VM1, you install and configure the following services:

• A web server

• A DNS server

VM1 has the effective network security rules shown in the following exhibit.

Based on this configuration, select the option that correctly completes the following statement:

"Internet users _________________________________________."

options.A: can connect to only the DNS server on VM1
options.B: can connect to only the web server on VM1
options.C: can connect to the web server and the DNS server on VM1
options.D: cannot connect to the web server and the DNS server on VM1

explanation: can connect to only the web server on VM1 is correct because the web server uses port 80, which is not blocked by any of the inbound security rules. However, Rule2 (with priority 100) explicitly denies access to ports 50-60 for all protocols, including port 53, which is used by the DNS service. Since port 53 is blocked by Rule2, internet users cannot connect to the DNS server on VM1 but can still connect to the web server. Can connect to only the DNS server on VM1 is incorrect because port 53 for DNS is blocked by Rule2. Can connect to the web server and the DNS server on VM1 is incorrect because the DNS port (53) is blocked. Cannot connect to the web server and the DNS server on VM1 is incorrect because the web server on port 80 is still accessible.

The web server on port 80 is already accessible, as it falls outside the range that was blocked by Rule2. Therefore, with Rule2 deleted, internet users would be able to connect to both the web server (on port 80) and the DNS server (on port 53). Can connect to only the DNS server on VM1 is incorrect because port 80 for the web server is also accessible. Can connect to only the web server on VM1 is incorrect because port 53 for DNS would also be accessible once Rule2 is deleted.
